Mr. Speaker, for the last few days I have been busy working in my constituency. It has been brought to my attention that on every day in my absence the government Whip, the hon. member for Calgary West, has mentioned my absence from the House of Commons. He knows, as we all know, that this is a practice that we do not follow. I notice that the Chair has permitted that at every occasion and has not reminded the government Whip of that fact.
I understand that today is not the day to pursue the question and the allegations that the hon. member has made against me. I look forward to Monday when presumably we will get into an Albertan version of a parliamentary shootout. I do not plan to bow to any pressure from the government or from the hon. member for Calgary West in terms of supporting a special justice system for members of Parliament or a two-tier justice system. I do not plan to support that in any way or ever, regardless of the pressure brought against myself or my colleagues in the New Democratic Party.
I understand that today we will not be proceeding with the matter that has been raised every day in my absence. However, I want to say I am looking forward with a great deal of anticipation to Monday where I can reveal, presumably with my other colleagues, all of the story behind this initiative by the government to create a two-tier justice system, giving special privileges to members of Parliament.

The House resumed from Friday, October 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Valcourt that Bill C-74, an act to amend the Fisheries Act and to amend the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

October 19, 1990
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I rise to talk on this bill this morning. I am very sincere when I say I do want to speak on it because it is a bill that affects most of my constituents. I know that it affects a lot of Newfoundlanders and all other Canadians involved in the fisheries.
What I plan to do this morning is give a bit of the background as to precisely what is happening with Bill C-74. I want to give the details of precisely what is happening with respect to the guts of the legislation. Then I want to provide a few editorial comments bearing in mind that this is the second reading and from here it goes on to committee. If we are anticipating hearings at the commitee stage, I would certainly believe and hope that my points would be taken account of in the commitee work.
At the outset I would like to say that his bill is essentially made or devised to increase the penalties for the incursions of fish habitat, essentially to make it more difficult with stiffer fines and longer jail sentences for those people who do not obey the Fisheries Act.
The Fisheries Act has been around for a long time. It was passed by Parliament in 1868 and, in short, it is a legal authority for the government to conserve and protect fish habitat where the fish live, swim, spawn, grow and are caught, and to control and manage Canada's fisheries.
To keep pace with the changing conditions the act has been amended more than 40 times in the past 122 years.
I think every member in this House is aware that the fisheries has undergone a tremendous amount of change in the past 10 years. It seems to me that it is always going through change, but I think more dramatically since the early eighties. We have had the Kirby report, the Harris report, the Hache report, and adjustment programs. The Senate has studied it and put out two reports. There has been a tremendous amount of change in the fisheries programs, in the licensing and in the regulations. This is just another attempt to improve. How perfect and how much of an improvement it will achieve, that will be the subject of my remarks.
The proposed changes, as I suggested earlier, will make the scale of fines and penalties for fisheries violations consistent with those that are contained in other legislation. This is the Fisheries Act. There is also the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, which essentially looks after foreign fishing, and there is the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. There are certain fines and measures in these acts that were inconsistent with the Fisheries Act, which as I understand contains the domestic fisheries.
One of the reasons this bill has been put forward is to put the domestic fisheries on a par with and to make it equivalent or equal to the environmental business and the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act that pertain to foreigners. I will speak more about that later.
It is not a cure-all, but it will provide a part of the solution. There is serious need in the fishing community, as a whole, to be protected from any activities, especially illegal activities that increase the stress on Canada's fishery and may even endanger the livelihood of entire communities, the examples of which we have unfortunately have seen more and more in the past three or four years.
Of equal priority, those responsible for altering or damaging the fish habitat will face much stiffer deterrents under the proposed legislation for violations. Some activities that have the potential for harming fish habitat areas include logging, pulp and paper processing, industrial emissions that enter fish habitat areas, and bridge and rural construction.
The bill also responds to real concerns about the unreliability of the data that can be obtained under the current act, since both the sources of the information and the ability to verify it are very limited.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that one of the difficulties as exposed in the Harris report and one of the difficulties that has emerged between the optimistic projections of the Kirby report of a 400,000 tonne total allowable catch and the present less than 100,000 or in the 90,000 tonne range which is essentially one-quarter of what we had been looking at less than a decade ago, has been the scientific data. While it is not my intention here nor will I castigate scientists, fish science like predicting the weather is a very inexact science. It relies on a tremendous amount of data for which we have not had the resources, either in manpower, in collection vehicles or
October 19, 1990

the records, to be able to support it. This bill does address the data collection aspect, and hopefully will improve the fairness and predictability for all concerned.
I was given to understand that these amendments reflect the concerns and the comments, both oral and written, of individual fishermen and their association. I must confess at the outset to having some reservations about that myself. I got off the phone as recently as 25 minutes ago to fishermen in my riding. None of them are too familiar with Bill C-74.
While I believe the Atlantic Fisheries Council and other organizations were briefed on the progress of what was going on, I consider a briefing somewhat different than a consultation. A briefing is: "This is what is happening", and consultation is: "This is what we are proposing. What would you like to see put into this?"
I regret to announce that once more I do not believe the considerable knowledge of the fishermen experts, who really after all are the best scientists when it comes to who are most involved and who are most affected by this, once again has not really been accounted for as much as I would be given to believe, had I read the propaganda that was put out by the government. However, I will say, on the other side of the coin, that those to whom I spoke believe that there is a need for stiffer fines for those people who are out to break the laws and, because of the need to conserve fish stocks, that is of tremendous concern to everyone.
I think this year I have attended a total of five conferences with a great number of fishermen and, if there is any such thing as the pendulum turning, my understanding as a politician from probably the largest fishing riding in Canada, the 295, is that fishermen are now saying: "Let us do what we need to do to conserve the stocks so that our total allowable catch will improve and that the fish stocks will improve over time". Mr. Speaker, that is the background. I am not going to go through all the details but I will give you some examples of what we are looking at.
Right now, we have a maximum fine of $5,000 or 12 months imprisonment on summary conviction for a general fisheries offence. That is going up to $100,000 on summary conviction and to $500,000 on indictment, with the court option of up to one year imprisonment on summary conviction, that is a summary trial, and two
Government Orders
years on indictment. What we are looking at is a tremendous, quantum jump in fines and in jail terms.
For the obstruction of a fishery officer, the fine is now $100 or six months. It is going up to $100,000 on summary conviction and, again, $500,000 on indictment. For the alteration of fish habitat, and I spoke to this in my introductory comments, there is a fine of up to $5,000 now and it is going up to $300,000 on summary conviction and on indictment it could go up to $1 million. One million dollars seems awfully high but when we look at what is involved, the loss of people's livelihoods as well as whole communities, then I do not think it is that unreasonable. However, I will speak to those points in a few moments.
Mr. Speaker, I made reference to the Hache report and the Harris report. In the Hache report, which came out about four or five months ago, it was noted that the maximum fine of $5,000 for illegal groundfishing is looked on by the industry as the cost of doing business. In other words, one gets fined, pays the fine and gets on with it. I do not think that is right, quite frankly, and I think I am supported by most of the fishermen who will be watching this and who will read the presentation which I am making.
The report also noted that enforcement can be made more effective and less costly by focusing on the consequence of breaking the rules. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans did a statistical analysis and they show that the levels of fines, on conviction, average about 5 per cent of the maximum. Thus, while the maximum was $5,000 the fines often averaged $250.
The Hache report also observed that the motivation to misreport the areas and species fished was high. I do not have first-hand knowledge of that, I have to take into consideration what the report says.
The task force was told repeatedly by industry participants that they believed the data was flawed and, in the case of commercial data, the accuracy of the information received by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans was considered questionable, due to the large-scale misre-porting and enforcement problems. Recommendations were made that would, essentially, amend the fisheries regulations in such a way that this would be redressed and, in effect, this is what we are seeing right now.

October 19, 1990

Mr. Speaker, the Hache report essentially referred to the Gulf and Fundy areas, as I understand it. I am much more familiar with the Harris report. It noted the misreporting of catches, bycatches, discard rates, and other significant inaccuracies in the commercial catch data. Dr. Harris emphasized that a vital aspect of management strategy must be the improvement of the quality of data used in the assessment.
Dr. Harris made two recommendations that pertain directly to this bill. The first one was that the Government of Canada should urge the appropriate authorities to treat violations of fisheries regulations, aimed at conservation, as a serious offence and to ensure that penalties imposed upon convicted violators be sufficiently onerous to fully offset any potential gains from violation. The second point was that the department should expand its data collection to improve the knowledge of effort levels and factors influencing the data of inshore fisheries and landing records.
I am going to give the House a record of the fisheries violation summary. 1988 is the last year for which complete statistics are available. The total number of convictions for fisheries violations in Canada were 3,325 which was an increase of 28 per cent over the previous years. The fines totalled $810,242, which was an increase of 91 per cent during that period.
In the Atlantic region that I am particularly concerned about, Mr. Speaker, the convictions totalled 1,366 with fines amounting to $489,759, an average of $358 per violation, as compared to the average, which I mentioned earlier, of $250.
For the record, in the Pacific region, the convictions were 1,959, amounting to $320,483 in fines, making an average fine of $266 and for sports fishing it turns out to be $90. Habitat convictions total 11, with an average fine of $3,135. That is all very well and it gives the background, some facts and figures.
I again note that we are at second reading. I have a number of reservations about this bill. The first one is that the present surveillance area and the increase in the surveillance area are both centred in the inshore sector.
I had a look at the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program last night. As noted by the hon. member for St. John's East some time ago when speaking on this bill,
surveillance has been allocated $57.5 million. I certainly laud that greatly because I have spoken in this House many times concerning the lack of surveillance. I laud this, but I still have some concerns for reasons that I will point in a few moments.
The government is chartering one offshore vessel in Newfoundland and five inshore vessels, so once again, Mr. Speaker, the focus of the activities is going to be on the inshore. I would be less than totally honest if I did not point out that I am aware of the observer program in the offshore which kind of makes up for the lack of patrol vessels. It is not all of one or nothing of the other, but it is my judgment that we should still strive to have a better balance for the offshore control in surveillance against the inshore.
The second point I have is that while the industry and fishermen have generally supported tougher legislation, I have a reservation that at least in my riding and for areas that I have spoken about, fishermen associations, have not really been consulted in the final form of the legislation. I do hope that during the committee stage that fishermen associations and the unions will be heard of to give their experience and their considerable knowledge so that we can tighten up the regulations even in a more just manner.
The question we really have to ask ourselves is that while tougher penalties are necessary, will the proposed legislation accomplish what it is intended to do, which essentially is to help the stocks be preserved, and, in our case, to grow.
The third reservation I have is that I think the government still lacks a comprehensive strategy to apprehend foreign violators, particularly American fishermen on the Canadian side of Georges Bank.
I do not want to relive the incident again, but I am sure that members of the House and anybody involved in fishing and enforcement recalls the very sad incident on December 11 last year when the U.S. scallop dragger, The Concordia, having been chased by the warship Saguenay, turned around and rammed the Saguenay. It is not the way it is supposed to be. It is supposed to be the warship that is supposed to ram the fishing vessel but it did not quite work out that way.

The first Friday.

Seriously, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to use warships to chase draggers, we have to be sure we do not lose the business. We have to make sure we are fully equipped, we need a good set-up and good communications. No one is laying blame in this case. I think the whole business of foreign overfishing and legitimate foreign fishing-and I will speak to this for one minute-inside the 200-mile limit, the other side of the House, and for a reason that I can understand, say: "Well, look, you Liberals are the ones that actually allowed the foreign fishing. You are the ones that gave the licences". I cannot deny that. I was not here at the time but that is fair enough. I accept that sort of criticism. When those foreign licences were given the total allowable catch was in the vicinity of 400,000

October 19, 1990

tonnes. Today, it is one-quarter that. I could not logically agree that we should continue to maintain the same foreign legitimate fishing inside our 200-mile limit while people cannot catch fish in their own home territories.
We are the only country in the world that gives away our main source of industry to other countries and watches them actually catch it. All I am asking is for a reduction commensurate with the total allowable catch, and it should follow some kind of a parallel graph. I do not think that is too much to ask.
My point is that when we talk about enforcing regulations on our own fishermen in our own domestic waters and fines up to $100,000, then we have to look at the whole picture.
There is another aspect here about which I am concerned. The bookkeeping requirements are extremely stringent. I put this to any reasonable member of the House: In Section 61, which I looked at last night, it states that fishermen and purchasers will be required to keep records of the number, the size, the weight, the sex, the species, the product form, or other particulars of any fish caught. Mr. Speaker, if you can imagine an open boat on a stormy day, and a fisherman in his oilskins with three or four crew members catching 30,000 pounds- they are quite capable of catching 30,000 pounds of fish, that is from 8,000 to 10,000 codfish-and they have to go through the sex, the size, the colour, the description, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Mr. Speaker, I believe that is too stringent. I really do.
Are you calling time, Mr. Speaker?

The other point I want to make before I come to a conclusion is that I would not want to see a salmon, not being tagged or being tagged improperly, have the maximum fine invoked. We have got to ensure that some kind of judgment is applied by these well intentioned fisheries officers. How do we legislate for judgment? In the committee hearings, I think we will have to look at that.
Again, on the business of surveillance, I would have to point out that, if we are looking at the over-all picture of surveillance in Canada., we use 23 maritime aircraft for 60,000 linear miles of coast. The Japanese use 250
aircraft for 228 miles of coastline and the Dutch use 17 aircraft for 5,000 miles. What that amounts to is that the Dutch use the fewer aircraft to look at 5,000 linear miles compared to our 60,000 linear miles, and the Japanese use ten times as many aircraft to look after somewhere in the vicinity of less than 1 per cent of the mileage that we have.
It is an indication of what we need to do to tighten up our surveillance. I am hoping that this will be looked at in the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak a second time. However, since you have been gracious enough to give me an opportunity to pose a question to my colleague, I will certainly afford myself of that opportunity.
Does the hon. member believe, as I do, that there is a need for consultations with regard to the implementation of this particular bill? Does he believe that we have to have before the committee representations from all fisheries organizations on both coasts, particularly those in Atlantic Canada, namely the Maritime Fishermen's
Government Orders
Union, in order to alleviate their fears, that this bill is not, in any way, intended to be discriminatory against the inshore fishery? I think we would need those kinds of individuals at the committee to get evidence which would suggest otherwise, and if indeed it is the opposite, that corrective measures be taken. Would the hon. member concur with that observation?

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your indulgence. I am very serious about this because the hon. member has raised a very important point. I alluded to it in my introductory remarks.
I have a concern that in the well-intentioned discharge of the legislation as the proposed bill now stands, it is my belief that the inshore fishermen would suffer unduly because, essentially, the enforcement action would be focused on them. I am not suggesting that inshore fishermen break the laws any more or less than offshore fishermen. What I am suggesting is that most inshore fishermen, and I am talking about the close inshore fishermen, are closer to the surveillance of fisheries officers who meet them when they come back to the wharf. Fisheries officers have a better means of getting to them when they are hauling their traps. They are small and independent businessmen. They do not work for corporations. A fisherman could be hit with a fine which before was less than $5,000 and averaged about $300, and all of a sudden one is looking at $10,000 or $20,000, which is well within the limits. This could put a small fisherman out of business very fast.
The fisherman's union that I am associated with, and I correspond and communicate with them frequently, has an inshore fisheries council. In response to the hon. member, I would strongly suggest that the Inshore Fisherman's Council and the associations that represent inshore fishermen make sure that they have an input into this in the committee stage and that the judgment that is applied and the amelioration of the bill in committee stage before third reading will be taken into account. Then the inshore fishermen will not be unnecessarily pinned down by this legislation.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin third reading debate on Bill C-37, an act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute.
Since the earliest days of history, the language of a community has always been its most vibrant cultural legacy. In this country, with its many language communities, the legacy is as rich as it is diverse.
Canada's linguistic resources are an inalienable part of our national identity and they are the voice and expression of our multicultural character. In a modern world, they are a vital and indispensable resource for the future.
The decision to create the institute was the result of thoughtful consultations with key leaders and groups in the heritage language field, along with Canadians from every region of the country. It was their support, people across the country, and their active involvement that brought us where we are today in the establishment of this institute.
I am proud that the government has taken the leadership in responding directly and in such a concrete way to the cause of more effective ways to support heritage language learning in the country.
The consultations that helped to give shape to the institute were an invaluable source of information and
inspiration. These discussions also indicated that many language communities are still isolated from each other and that instructional standards continue to vary greatly from one community to the next. It was clear from the discussions that the existing structures and approaches simply are not adequate for the challenges and the opportunities ahead of us and, if we were to achieve a more effective use of heritage languages in Canada, that we would have to address fundamental deficiencies.
Leading experts in organizations working in the field, along with government officials, concluded that the only way to improve the situation was to introduce more innovative ways to link our communities. We have to find new ways to capitalize on what does work, replace what does not, and bring forward new ideas and methods that can be shared across the country.
Canada's linguistic communities called for a national resource, founded on co-operation and partnership. They wanted an institution that would understand the practical workings of these local language schools and one would appreciate just how important it is for students, whether they are Ethiopian or Ukrainian Canadians, to have modern text books that foster the learning process, not ones that hindered it.
That new vision is the very essence of this legislation, Bill C-37. It is not an ethereal vision, not one of ivory towers where lofty academics muse about the state of languages in abstract terms. That is not our vision, not at all.
I know that many Canadians who volunteer their time to support their heritage languages do so in the most natural and modest way. The instructors in our communities week by week achieve the most remarkable results. In the process, these volunteers do this country a very great service indeed in providing our young people with language skills promoting their cultural identity and later to achieve opportunities in the international and global world in which we all share.
In establishing the institute, we understand that Canadians want and demand that all government initiatives be fiscally responsible. That is why we have modelled the Heritage Languages Institute with this viewpoint in mind. In particular, we realize that people working in the heritage language field do not want the government to squander scarce resources by over-staffing the institute
October 19, 1990

or by establishing a large alienating building in which to house it.
The mandate of this institute and the mandate of the people who work in the heritage language field is to sustain and to strengthen Canada's heritage languages. In practical terms the institute will be responsible for developing Canadian-orientated materials in-house and for disseminating these materials throughout our many language communities. The institute will act as a clearing house, seeking to correct the uneven access to teaching resources and replacing it with greater uniformity and higher standards.
The actual institute itself, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you personally will be pleased to hear, will be located in Edmonton. From the beginning we have committed ourselves to creating an institute without walls, a place where language communities and associations from every region will feel right at home. Wherever the community is, they belong.
Quality research and materials are only as effective as the teachers who use them. For this reason the institute will do its part to help to improve the standard of heritage language instruction by developing more effective training methods and courses.
In terms of financial support, the institute will receive $6.5 million over five years and as a charitable foundation, financial support for the institute may also come from the private sector and community sources, as well as from provincial and territorial governments.
Part of the federal government's financial support will be directed to an endowment fund. In this way we will make the institute a permanent, lasting testimony to the promise of Canada's linguistic resources.
The doors of this institute will always be open to all who wish to support its work. I like to think that above these doors will be the names of every one of Canada's language communities, if not in reality then at least in the minds of the people who work there. As the staff of the institute go out into the communities, they will be helpful in sharing their ideas and working together.
In conclusion, I would like to thank all those who have participated in bringing this Bill C-37 to third reading, all those witnesses who came to the committee and, indeed, the members of this House who were members of the legislative committee of Bill C-37 who worked together to strengthen and improve the legislation that is before

us. I know that they share with me a sense of how important this institute will be and what it can achieve.
Recently I had an opportunity to speak to one of the leaders of the heritage language instruction. He called the establishment of this heritage language institute a crown jewel. We look forward to this institute being operational very soon. It is a challenging mandate for any institute to serve as a trustee of this nation's linguistic resources, not only for today but for generations to come.
With the support and talent of Canadians, we share the same larger vision. It will achieve its objectives and become a source of promise and lasting achievement for all people.
I urge all members of the House of Commons to pass this bill on third reading quickly in order for us to establish this institute as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, establishing a Canadian Heritage Languages Institute is in itself a step in the right direction. Cultural groups and language teachers feel it is important to have a centre where documentation on language learning is collected, catalogued and, above all, distributed across the country.
On the other hand, we must avoid duplication and ensure that the Institute is sensitive to the needs of the community and regularly updates its information and existing teaching materials.
If the Institute is to be truly effective, it must communicate on a continuing basis with all cultural groups in order to establish a relationship based on co-operation and trust.
Mr. Speaker, the Institute's mandate is a broad one, especially since it is to be an institution without walls that will serve the entire country. I have some questions about this aspect.
How does the present government, with a budget initially designed to respond to the needs of Western Canada, according to the reports of Professors Kreisel and Batts, plan to respond to the expectations of an entire country? We cannot afford to let a lack of funds hamper the Institute in its work. No region in Canada should be penalized because the Conservative govern-

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
merit has decided all research will be directed from Edmonton.
Mr. Speaker, according to what has been said by both authors of reports and the groups that were consulted, the Canadian Eleritage Languages Institute was supposed to be one of two new Canadian institutes that would complement the one already in place in Toronto. In fact, at the time, the plan was that one institute would be based in Edmonton, to respond more specifically to the needs of the West in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, while another institute would be established in Quebec to meet the needs of the East.
These two entities were to focus mainly on applied research and developing teaching tools, thus complementing the work done by the Toronto institute. All three were to be complementary and work together, to save time and avoid duplication.
Thanks to their strategic locations, the three institutes would have been in a position to respond to specific regional needs, since heritage languages are not necessarily the same in Halifax and Vancouver, and thus develop teaching techniques adapted to the target population.
According to Bill C-37, however, there will be a single headquarters in Edmonton that will serve all provinces. An institution without walls, with a budget originally intended to meet the needs of four provinces, will now have to respond to the needs of the entire country. It will be interesting to see how it will manage this "tour de force".

The Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and Citizenship will have to stay alert and follow closely the setting up of the institute to ensure the representation of all parts of Canada on the board of directors. It will be crucial in the orientation the institute will take, thus the need of having people from different groups, different areas of work and different regions of the country.
If the institute is to serve the people, it must be representative of the people. It makes no logic sense to have an institute that is supposed to serve the needs of
the Canadian population if that body is not responsible to the community that is to use it as a resource centre.
The mandate of the institute is broad. Because of this, it could easily become another elite paper-producing organization. This must not happen. The institute must never lose sight of grassroots people; those who are working in the field and have been creating material throughout the years, those who know and live the problems, those who need back-up. That is why the institute is there.
Here again, I have very serious doubts about this government's intentions. Let us not forget that this is the same government that gave $14 million to teach Canada's business elite how to speak various languages of Pacific Rim countries. Where are the priorities of this government? They love to talk about less government intervention and budget cuts. Unfortunately for the youth of this country, the government only remembers this fact when it is dealing with women, youth and native issues.
When it comes to its friends in the business community, it opens its purse strings. Mr. Speaker, I must say that I find this completely unacceptable.

If, as the Minister of State has repeated so often, the $4.1 million cut is actually only $30 per student, if the Conservative government feels that the amount is so insignificant, why are schools closing down because they did not get that grant? Is this the way the government shows it cares about the needs of the people? And if so, what guarantee do we have that the institute will do better than the government? How do we make sure all groups can benefit from institute resources, not only a select few in major urban centres or others with access to technological facilities? The institute simply cannot afford to discriminate against any group no matter how important or where it is located. This will be a major challenge which the institute will have to live up to.
Canada is again going through times of crises and tensions. The coming months and years will give us the opportunity to promote multiculturalism throughout Canada. Wherever people may come from they must be made to feel they are part of Canada. The ideal is to be Canadian without having to negate one's own cultural
October 19, 1990

heritage. This is a major challenge, and the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute is one of the tools we have at hand for the job.
The Minister of State may well be sincere, Mr. Speaker, but we do entertain doubts about the motives of the Conservative government: even before the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship saw the light of day, they reduced the budget of the future department. How can we believe the government when it claims to be promoting harmony and then turns around and tells people who need grants to maintain their cultural heritage that no funds are available? How is it possible for an institute slated for Western Canada and expected to serve the whole country to meet the urgent and basic needs of heritage languages schools with an annual budget of a little over $1.2 million?

Mr. Speaker, we understand that there must be budget restraints, but should we cut on a department that has yet to become a reality, a department that has, as a mandate, to help create harmony among the people of Canada? In this summer of discontent, some of the most disturbing facts have been an increase in intolerance against various communities in our great country. The only response that this government gave was its silence.
The Prime Minister and his cabinet refused to call Parliament back to deal with various issues, as Canada seemed to be swept over with feelings of resentment. The vast majority of this hatred is directed at this government. Unfortunately, some of this discontent was redirected to various minority groups. Instead of coming out with concrete actions to assist in the creation of harmonious race relations across Canada, this government has done nothing, except cut funding to heritage language schools that help in the preservation and promotion of harmonious, cross-cultural understanding.
In B.C., without federal funding, some of these heritage schools will close. Some already have. The schools are the reason why this government is trying to establish the heritage language institute. It seems illogical to establish an institute that is supposed to act as a resource centre for the schools that this government is forcing to close. That is why I seriously doubt this government's
commitment to either this issue or others relating to racial and cultural harmony in this country.

On October 27, Mr. Speaker, children, teachers, parents and directors of Ottawa region heritage language schools will hold a demonstration on Parliament Hill. They will present note books from every school containing handwritten letters and children's drawings protesting against their reduced budgets. Before and after the demonstration we hope to present a number of petitions in the House to bring pressure on the government.

Mr. Speaker, it has come to my attention that remarks I made in the House on October 16 are being inappropriately used, or even distorted, by Liberals and Conservatives in Manitoba.
Unfortunately, unhappiness with elements of the environmental record of the former NDP government, by which I still stand, caused me to generalize unfairly about its record on Rafferty-Alameda.

Any suggestion, therefore, aided by my comments that the NDP government inadequately responded to the deal between McMillan and Devine is completely out of line and dishonest. Indeed, if Gary Filmon is into quoting me, I ask him to quote from Hansard page 14231 of the same day, October 16, in which I referred to the

October 19, 1990
refusal of his Tory government to take strong action, given all the things that have taken place since he came to power.
Furthermore, I have had the opportunity since 1988 to work on Rafferty and other environmental issues with Gary Doer, and it is precisely because of the new and deeper commitment that he brings to environmental issues that we did so well in the last election.

Between October 12 and 21, Mr. Speaker, we celebrate our first week of science and technology.
Because science and technology offer many advantages we should be more conscious of the role they play in our daily lives and in our domestic economy with a view to promoting scientific culture in Canada.
It will stand as a challenge to improve our standard of living, boost the competitiveness of our industries, and open up interesting career opportunities. We will be much better prepared to face up to and overcome the many obstacles which threaten our environment.
Mr. Speaker, let us make a common effort during this week of science and technology to raise the interest of all Canadians in the key role of science in our society and to make Canada more competitive on the international market.

Mr. Speaker, by the government's own count, 1,500 fishermen and plant workers on the Labrador coast are without income this winter, and this government evidently does not give a damn. Because of the worst failure in the fishery in years, Labrador fishermen and plant workers, many of whom are aboriginal, do not even have 10 qualifying weeks let alone the 14 now required for unemployment insurance.
Once again Labrador fishermen find themselves in an emergency while the federal government stands idly by. If special funds are not put in place this month, it will be too late. Even the minister's own Industrial Adjustment Committee has documented the seriousness of the situation and called for an emergency response program.
This has nothing to do with Bill C-21, because even if Bill C-21 passes, hundreds of Labrador people will still not qualify for unemployment insurance. The people of Labrador are full Canadians and are entitled to the support of their government.
I call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration to announce an emergency response program for Labrador and to do it now.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday was Persons Day, and I think it appropriate to recognize a recent contribution to women's equality.
The Federal Solicitor General has announced that the maximum security prison for women in Kingston is closing. In its place, the government is going to build five regional facilities for federally sentenced women, including a healing lodge for aboriginal inmates. This action came about because of the task force recommendation on federally sentenced women.
I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate all those within government and in non-government organizations who worked so hard to produce what I believe to be a very progressive, forward looking initiative that will help to improve the quality of life for incarcerated women.
Many years ago, Agnes Macphail, the first woman MP started the fight to close this prison. This government has finally taken this important step to building a better future for women and society as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has disappointed the disabled community yet again.
October 19, 1990

Earlier in the week he rebuffed a request by the Thalidomide Victims Association of Canada for a compensation package of about $48.9 million, spread over 30 years, for thalidomide victims.
Canada is the only country that has neither acknowledged its responsibility to the victims nor settled legal liabilities with them. Canadians will remember that their government not only did not prevent the sale of thalidomide, but it failed to withdraw it from the market quickly enough when its harmful effects had already been scientifically verified.
Victims have to live with their physical deformities and handicaps, but their families will not always be available to provide them support. The $18.9 million package would provide for current and long-term accommodations to permit the integration of victims in society, but the minister holds firm and obdurate when compassion and justice cry for action.
Yet just next to him his colleague, the minister of energy, was able to squeeze a mere $602 million in grants and cash payments to suffering oil companies last year alone. We ask: Where are this minister's priorities?

Mr. Speaker, everyone claims a little Irish in their blood, and New Brunswickers are no exception.
Next year our province will play host to the International Gathering of the Irish in North America, and we will be having shamrock citizens with us from around the world.
This is another unique opportunity, both for New Brunswick and for Canada, to demonstrate that we really are a nation for all the world, for all cultures, for all races, for all people.
Just consider the human blend and interchange to take place when Canada's officially bilingual province, New Brunswick, meets and mixes with the world's favourite adopted strain, the Irish: "Sure-'twill be like a morn in spring".
This is an early invitation for every member of this House to come to New Brunswick between July 19 and August 3, 1991. There you will share the best of Irish
humour; there you will see the best of Irish art; there you will sing the best of Irish songs; all in a setting of true Canadian hospitality at its best.
Just this week we had an advance visit by an Irishman from Baie Comeau. Already Irish eyes are smiling and Irish hearts are happy.
Please come and join us next summer.

Mr. Speaker, the great leveller, the great equalizer among children worldwide is when a child acquires the ability to read and then has reading materials made readily accessible to him or to her.

October 19, 1990
There is no other single skill which will open up the world of knowledge and dispel the darkness of ignorance and thus relieve human hardship through enlightenment more than the ability to read effectively.

Mr. Speaker, the Cash Flow Enhancement Program will enable farmers to secure interest-free cash advances during the current 1990-91 crop year. Each producer will be able to secure up to $50,000 interest free on the security of his undelivered grain.
I want to thank the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds for their prompt response to the serious cash flow problems resulting from lack of opportunity to market the current
crop. The cash flow enhancement program enables farmers to get some immediate cash on grain they have produced but cannot sell.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday the Minister of Finance said in the House, "We brought in a higher interest rate precisely to fight inflationary pressures". Yet the goods and services tax, the GST, according to the figures of the Department of Finance, will increase inflation by more than 20 per cent above current levels.
I ask the Deputy Prime Minister this. Why is the government working at cross purposes? Why is it pursuing two contradictory policies, on the one hand keeping up interest rates allegedly to fight inflation and on the other hand, forcing the GST on Canadians when it knows that GST will greatly increase inflation?

That has been known right from the beginning. That is not news and that is not something that is shocking or the Leader of the Opposition is not revealing something that is new. That has been said all along and of course would be taken into consideration in setting any kind of interest rates that are set from week to week by the Bank of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):

Will the minister undertake that the Governor of the Bank of Canada will not be allowed to increase interest rates even further to counter the inflation caused by the GST?

In other words, Mr. Speaker, could the minister give the House the assurance that the Governor of the Bank of Canada will not further increase interest rates in response to inflationary pressures caused by his GST?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada is following a policy to wring inflation out of the economy. It is very important that the inflationary pressures are wrung out.
For example, in July and August, average wage increases in this country were 6.1 per cent. That causes, of course, inflationary pressures. The inflation rate has held fairly steady at 4.2 per cent as was announced this morning. We are encouraged by that, but there is still too much inflationary pressure in the economy.
The Bank of Canada and the Minister of Finance, unlike the opposition, do not have knee-jerk reactions to what is going on in the economy. It is a policy that is followed to wring inflation out of this economy and to assure that interest rates come down and stay down, not like in the days when the Liberals were in power and we saw inflation at 13 per cent and interest rates at between 20 per cent and 25 per cent. We are not going to let that happen to this country.

Mr. Speaker, the government's approach to economic policy is clearly perverse. At a time when the government's own trade figures show that our exports are falling, the government made a deal which allows the Varity Corporation to close the Kelsey plant in Windsor with a loss of more than 500 export related jobs.

The important thing about the Kelsey-Hayes closing is that bad as it is, the workers have at least been offered a deal which is better than they might have been offered under other circumstances.

My question to the Acting Prime Minister is: Why did Premier Bob and his friend, Brian, cave in?

Will the government start making the tough decisions and admit that it has been wrong? Will it admit that there is a recession? Will it admit that high interest rates

are, in fact, hurting this economy? Will it admit that the Canadian dollar has to decline to get-

That you created.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
No, we have not made a mistake in our economic policy. We know people are hurting. In his budget in February, the Minister of Finance said there would be a slowdown in the economy
and a slight increase in unemployment. That prediction was made by the government in the Minister of Finance's budget, so that is not a surprise, that was expected. At the same time, the policies of this government are for the long term, to get interest rates down permanently, to get inflation down so that the economy can grow in a balanced manner. That is what this is all about.
God help us if the NDP were in power, it would be slapping band-aids here, there, and everywhere, and inflation would be running out of control today.

Mr. Speaker, surely the government is prepared to admit that the economic situation that we find ourselves in today is different than existed at the time when the government first contemplated the GST. Surely it is willing to admit that.
Is the government completely closed-minded about changing its mind on the GST? Is it completely closed-minded about listening to the small business community, to labour, and to almost everyone in the whole country, except itself, who think that it may be time to reconsider the wisdom of imposing the GST in the new economic circumstances that we find? Is it going to be at least reconsidered?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Weiner that Bill C-37, an Act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before Question Period, on October 27, children, teachers, parents and administrators of heritage language schools in the Ottawa area will hold a demonstration on Parliament Hill.
On this occasion, there will be a presentation of handwritten letters and children's drawings from each school, protesting cutbacks in funding to the schools.
Mr. Speaker, both before and after this event, we shall regularly table petitions in the House, in order to put pressure on the government.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to see this institute become window dressing for a government that has left the cupboards of heritage language education bare. I must really question the effectiveness of this move and ask how much it can really do.
I am also concerned about funding for aboriginal languages. I am concerned that this government has cut funding for various native newspapers and publications. I am concerned that this government's policy does not satisfy the language needs of Canada's aboriginal people.
I would hope that all members of this House would support the private member's bill of my colleague from Western Arctic calling for the creation of a native language's institute.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, quality education is and remains the key to the future. The Institute must serve those people who wish to promote their cultural heritage and who are dedicated to sharing their knowledge with their peers. We in the Liberal Party support the establishment of this Institute, but we intend to watch the situation very closely to ensure that no region is neglected.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand at the third reading stage of Bill C-37, an act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute.
Every year we welcome thousands of immigrants to Canada from many different lands. Of course, if they do not speak English or French when they first arrive, it is essential that language training be a first priority in order for them to adjust quickly in Canada.
This requires adequate federal and provincial resources for English as a second language classes or French language classes so that children will have the extra help they need and schools will not be overburdened. In the city of Vancouver this is a very crucial concern at this time.
Adults of all ages, and I include women as well as men, who often have the priority for language training related to employment, must have language fluency to become Canadians. Elderly persons who come to Canada to

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
become a part of our society need opportunities for training in Canadian languages as well. This, I think, is the first language priority in multicultural Canada.
I must say before I speak to this bill that I regret very much that the federal government does not fulfil its responsibility to adequately finance language training in French or English for either adults or children.
The opportunity to maintain and learn heritage language also has been a very important component of Canadian multicultural policy. The government itself has repeated this objective often.
Language reflects culture, and young people need an opportunity to speak the language of their parents and of their grandparents, m order to appreciate their roots and to develop their identity, as part of becoming Canadians. It enriches all of us to have Canadian citizens who are fluent in second languages or, in some cases, in third languages. We can be very proud of the cosmopolitan, international character of our Canadian mosaic and our Canadian communities.
In my riding of Vancouver East, Mr. Speaker, I often visit heritage language schools, where children spent their Saturday mornings learning the language of their parents and their grandparents. Along with that, of course, they absorb the culture and reinforce their parental culture.
I want to pay tribute at this time to the hardworking teachers in these schools and in schools for heritage language classes right across the country. These teachers often work with very few resources and on low salaries.
Also I have known of children in my riding, and I am sure other members have similar experiences, who did not learn the language of their parents or grandparents. When they become teenagers, very often there are serious communication problems that create barriers between generations, and even lead to family breakdown.
Heritage language classes cost very little and they bring values to our society as well as to individuals. Therefore, we support the concept of a heritage language institute. Even more, we support the government subsidies. They are pretty small subsidies when you look
at individual classes that have in the past been given to heritage language schools.
We regret very much that the government eliminated $4.1 million for heritage language classes from its last budget. This not only denies their stated policy, but it has forced the closure of many schools. It is of major concern to ethnocultural groups across this country.
Bill C-37 which we are debating in its final stage today is to establish a Canadian heritage language institute, an institute to be based in Edmonton. It is very sad, and I think somewhat ironic, that on the one hand, while the government takes away $4.1 million from last year's budget for heritage language classes, on the other hand, it has decided to give a little token back in the form of $1.2 million, just a fraction of the budget for previous years and only over a five-year period, let us not forget, to provide research and to assist the very heritage language classes it is killing off in communities because of inadequate funding.
We are not opposed to establishing a heritage language institute but we do seriously question the government's priorities and the political motivation in this instance. It certainly appears that the institute is a token political gesture so that the government can save face for having cut funding to the first priority, which must be the very community classes that will provide heritage language and for which an institute would be established.
What is the purpose of the institute and what are some of the concerns that were expressed by most witnesses that appeared before the legislative committee? I would like to quickly summarize some of these.
The purpose of the institute, as stated in the bill, is to provide a resource centre for the production, acquisition, retention and dissemination of information related to heritage language classes, a research centre for conducting studies on all aspects of heritage languages and for setting standards on how they should be taught. I think most witnesses that we talked to and people who we have been in touch with across the country feel that this is a valuable service that is needed, provided you have the classes and the communities to use it. It also would provide a public relations centre for promoting heritage languages and maintaining liaison with governments and institutions.
October 19, 1990

Government Orders
The funding would be $6.5 million over five years and then, I assume, it would be terminated. Surely that must be a major concern for those who will on the board of this institute. Their headquarters will be in Edmonton. We do not object to this but I think it should be pointed out that according to an eminent researcher who consulted various groups and made proposals to the government, that one of the priorities that made Edmonton and western Canada a priority was the fact that heritage languages of western Canadians could be stressed. This should give particular priority to immigrants from Asian countries who have quite a different basic language base from European groups that came earlier to our country.
We agree that a resource centre of this kind will be valuable, provided that we are able to maintain frontline community services. I would like to mention a number of concerns that were expressed in committee, that have been expressed in letters and conversations that we had with a number of witnesses. These people have direct experience in heritage language classes. I would like to mention again that we debated this at great length with a number of very eloquent speakers at the last stage of amendments.
The point I would like to make is the very strong request that came from aboriginal organizations that the languages of founding peoples, the aboriginal peoples of Canada, be excluded from this bill. They must have support to establish a separate aboriginal language institute. This was debated in committee. We were glad to see that the reference to aboriginal languages as part of this particular institute was deleted. There was not an amendment added which we had strongly proposed, and which was requested from aboriginal organizations, that would specifically mention exclusion of aboriginal languages.
There were a number of very eloquent speeches made on the question of the need for recognition of aboriginal languages, with both the preservation and teaching of these very important languages that are unique to Canada and North America.
One of the major concerns and a continuing concern is the funding cuts to heritage language classes.
This was a concern of every witness who came to committee and many whom government members refused to hear. I think they were a little afraid to have the constant criticism from groups across the country.
In fact, I want to say that the Heritage Language Association of British Columbia has refused to support the Heritage Languages Institute until funding of classes is restored. Other witnesses supported Bill C-37, but called very strongly for reinstatement of funding to classes as a priority.
The Secretary of State, as I said earlier, despite receiving only a 5 per cent cut in its total 1990 budget, eliminated the $4.1 million annual subsidy to heritage language classes across the country. I want to repeat, as I have said many times and other speakers have said before in the House, that this means a 100 per cent funding cut for the 1,500 schools and 129,000 students who are learning 60 different languages. Many schools have had to close down as a result, and others have had to raise tuition fees which makes them inaccessible to children from low income families.
I want to mention, particularly, some of the more recent immigrant groups. I am thinking of immigrant groups from Asia and the Middle East, although there are not quite as many groups in my own community from that region. These are groups that have not had heritage language classes established and they do not have a curriculum. There should be priority special funding to establish classes for these newer language groups that have come to Canada.
There have been leaders of ethnocultural groups and heritage language associations and students and parents representing different languages from every region of Canada who have lobbied hard for the reinstatement of funding. I note that there is going to be a cross-Canada rally on Saturday, October 27, including a rally here on Parliament Hill, to express again the great concern that there is still on this matter. It will not go away.
The government must realize that groups are not going to forget about this and that they are going to keep insisting, as we are, that there must be federal responsibility for funding for heritage language classes. It is absolutely ridiculous that we can consider putting millions of dollars into an institute when the very classes

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
that are to be served by this institute are being quite undercut by this withdrawal of funding.
We are very concerned that the government really has very misguided priorities. The minister's rationale of course was that language classes should be a provincial responsibility. We hope the provincial governments will contribute, but let us not forget it is the federal government that has a responsibility for immigration and for multiculturalism. This falls directly within the responsibility of those two federal jurisdictional responsibilities.
Witnesses have also told us that there simply is not provincial funding and there never will be in many regions. I am sure in the Atlantic region this is true. In British Columbia, schools have closed because we do not have adequate provincial funding. I do not think the federal government can just slough this off and think that it is going to get away with it.
Another concern we have to look at is, while it sounds as if the $6.5 million over five years is a lot of money, actually, Mr. Speaker, when you break it down per year and think of it being ended at the end of five years, this is a pretty insufficient amount of money. One of the concerns that we have, and that witnesses had, is that it does not allow for any decentralizing of services of the institute to serve other regions. I know people in the province of Quebec, for example, will have concerns about this, as will people in other regions. Originally this institute was to focus on western needs, as I said, but as time progressed and as the bill came into being, the minister's interpretation has certainly been that this is established to serve all of Canada. I am not sure that it is possible to do that.
Dr. Kreisel, one of the researchers who conducted the feasibility study, said very strongly in committee that this institute should be an institute without walls. We do not need a lot of centralized, bureaucratic, academic institutions. We need the resources to go out and help people in the communities where they live and that will be able to use the funding and so on to be just as close to teachers and students in communities as is possible.
It should be a very practical institute and it should work very closely with people in the field and we would urge that this be a major focus of the institute.
I want to mention another question which came up a number of times. It was a very legitimate question. On the one hand, the government has taken all the federal funding away from community heritage language classes and, on the other hand, it has decided to give $65 million for the elite kind of training of business people, under Project 2000, related to the Minister for International Trade. The government has decided to give $65 million while $4.1 million has been taken away from community language classes where children can learn, as they are growing up and be fluent in these languages, particularly in Pacific Rim languages.
We feel very strongly that the learning of Pacific Rim languages, particularly those which are going to be useful in trade, are very, very important. But let us not kid ourselves. We have enough experience in teaching French as a second language to know that it is best to start learning the language at a younger age.
From an administrative point of view, it makes great sense to include the training needs for languages which will be needed for Pacific Rim trade, as part of this institute referred to in this bill that we are debating today. Why should it not be specializing in the languages that are necessary for trade, developing the kind of curriculum, teaching aids and supports for the establishment of practical classes for business people and others? We do not see the kind of priority for this elitist approach of putting $65 million toward training for business people, while taking away money from classes for children and not including these classes under this institute because they certainly will need the kind of resources that supposedly this institute will provide.
I want to make one final point that was part of the criticism of the whole process in the legislative committee on Bill C-37. It is important not to forget that, once again, opposition members worked very hard to try to bring amendments that would improve the bill. The government, as it has consistently done in other committees in which I have been involved in the multiculturalism area, refused to go along with amendments.
In particular, we had hoped that the government would accept amendments that would empower the institute to fund heritage language classes, as a desperate last attempt since the funds were being taken away from the other direct funding. Some of the witnesses we
October 19, 1990

questioned suggested this could be used especially for new languages which are not as well developed.
We also felt that there should have been an amendment, as I said, to assist in the teaching of the languages which would be beneficial to Canada's international trade and international relations. This amount of money then could have been integrated.
I would like to point out also that the government members on the committee also tried desperately hard to limit public input by refusing to hear regional witnesses. It was only after opposition members threatened to boycott meetings that they reconsidered. It is pretty disgraceful when these kinds of things happen.
I would like to quote quickly an excerpt from a letter that was received from the B.C. Heritage Language Association which reflected the concerns of many witnesses. They state: "The harsh reality for B.C. heritage language learners is that closures of heritage language schools is inevitable. We are affronted by the hypocrisy of removing grassroots support while giving to a potential mausoleum."
We will not vote against this bill because it has been our policy to support the establishment of the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute. However, once again, we ask the government to reinstate essential funding for heritage languages classes in communities as its first priority.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a very simple question. I would like to ask the member if the New Democratic Party is for this bill or against this bill? I could not make heads nor tails of what she was saying.

Mr. Speaker, as I stated in my remarks and in previous speeches that we made in the House, we will be supporting this bill reluctantly. We support the concept of an institute, but we do so with the expectation that the government will reinstate funding for heritage language classes.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to be able to speak to this act to establish a heritage languages institute.

My premise is that learning languages, whether the language happens to be English, French or any other
Government Orders
languages in Canada or on this planet, is a means of personal enrichment. I firmly believe that we should not neglect languages. Certainly not.

We all realize that in this country, English, as it should, has received a lot of attention and it must continue to do so. We recognize as well that the French language has increased in importance and significance and it has had more opportunities to develop, as it should.
We also have to admit and acknowledge that the treatment we have given to native languages and heritage languages has not at all been appropriate. It has been sadly lacking.
Why are languages so important to people and indeed to Canada. Rather than try to give you the reasons myself I want to quote from testimony given to house committees here. The first is from Eli Taylor, an elder of the Sioux Valley Reserve in Manitoba. He made the following points:
"Our native language embodies a value system about how we ought to live and relate to each other -It gives a name to relations among kin, to roles and responsibilities among family members, to ties with the broader clan group-There are no English words for these relationships because your social and family life is different from ours. Now if you destroy our language, you not only break down these relationships, but also you destroy other aspects of our Indian way of life and culture, especially those that describe man's connections with nature, the Great Spirit and the order of things. Without our language, we will cease to exist as a separate people.
In terms of heritage languages, I would like to quote some of the testimony given by Ms. Sarah Del Rosario, who is a heritage languages teacher with the United Council of Filipino Associations in Canada, who represented the Canadian Ethnocultural Council. She stated as follows:
These languages are a symbol of the fundamental respect to Canadian communities of origins other than French or English - they are central to the cultures and the cultural preservation and promotion of minority ethnocultural communities.
- they are a central aspect of Canadian multiculturalism as lived by families in towns across Canada-They assist in developing positive attitudes towards the national official languages policy. They assist young people in their ability to learn a third language, often the official language -As well, they greatly advance the international trading ability of Canada as more Canadians develop a detailed and enthusiastic knowledge of the languages, cultures, and norms of countries all over the world.

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
Let us go back to the institute. Why are we founding this institute? Why is it that we think this is a good idea? I have tried to argue that the preservation and learning of heritage languages is important from a number of perspectives. The cultural perspective because, as the world changes, we recognize that we need to learn to get along with each other, no matter what kind of linguistic, religious or other backgrounds we come from. This is of paramount importance to each and every one of us, whether we be Canadians or people from other countries.
We recognize as well from a social perspective that people with other languages often see problems rather differently than we do, but some of their approaches are in fact superior to our own. If we can protect and enhance their language, it will enrich us as well.
We know that from an economic perspective there are tremendous gains to be made in the preservation of language and culture. Let me give some examples of some of the languages that we have in Canada, and obviously I cannot cover them all, and some of the trade that we carry on with some of the home countries of those particular languages.
First, over 300,000 Canadians claim Chinese as their mother tongue. Canada's total trade with Hong Kong, the People's Republic of China and Taiwan exceeded $8.9 billion, the latest figures available. We have over
125.000	Canadians who claim Dutch as their mother tongue and we do roughly $2.2 billion worth of trade with Holland. Over 85,000 Canadians claim Spanish as then-mother tongue and if we look at the trade that we undertake with Spain, Mexico, Argentina, Peru and Venezuela, it amounts to almost $4 billion. Over 20,000 Canadians claim Korean as their mother tongue and if we look at the trade with North and South Korea, we have trade in the area of $3.5 billion. Over 160,000 Canadians claim Portuguese as their mother tongue and if you look at Portugal and Brazil, we have close to $2 billion in trade. Our total trade with Japan is almost $19 billion and there are, according to my statistics, roughly
20.000	Canadians who claim Japanese as their mother tongue.
Almost 500,000 Canadian citizens claim German as their mother tongue and if we look at our trade with West Germany it totals $5.6 billion. If we add Austria and East Germany, it exceeds $6 billion. Our trade with the U.S.S.R. is roughly $1.3 billion and if we look at
Canadians who claim Ukrainian, Russian, Estonian, Latvian and a number of languages from that particular group of countries, we have an important number indeed. Over one million Canadians claim Italian as their mother tongue and with Italy we do almost $3 billion worth of business.
Quite apart from the cultural benefits and the social benefits, there are serious and important economic benefits and I have given but a few examples. It would seem rather silly, ineffective, inefficient to try to teach those languages to people who already know them when we know full well that we will need them in the international markets of the world as the world changes quickly into a global community.

I would now like to discuss some very serious problems with this bill. First of all, people who were directly affected will never forgive this government for cutting more than $4 million in funding for courses taught in heritage languages. They were deeply hurt.
Also, is this a symbolic gesture or has a deep commitment been made? With there will be sufficient funds to ensure the Institute's mandate is carried out? Will the Board of Directors, when it represents from 50 to 60 members, include enough people with an interest in heritage languages?
Will the Institute realize that it will have to work together with various urban and rural communities, universities, people who teach these courses, families, young people and the not-so-young? Will it realize there are a number of groups that must be brought together so that their expertise can be used and we can truly benefit from their knowledge? This should not become an elitist institute that responds only to a single group.
It will also be necessary to make frequent assessments of the Institute's performance, in a manner that is fair and equitable. We want to ensure that the Institute is able to achieve the objectives it has been set, but I see no mechanism for doing so.

There are also very important explanations that must be given to the Canadian people with respect to this particular initiative. Let me give some examples. The English language community wonders why, as it should with some justification. What is this going to accomplish?
October 19, 1990

Is this the way we ought to be going? This explanation is needed just because of what is happening. The need is even compounded when one looks, for example, at The Free Press of October 7,1990, where the hon. member for Winnipeg South is referred to in a headline that reads: "Multiculturalism Policy Divisive, Dobbie says". It goes on to say that the policy is a waste of money. When you get comments like that from the government side, clearly that leads to confusion, frustration and anger.
What was the response on October 11 from the same newspaper headline: "Anti-Multiculturalism Remarks Rile Ethnic Leaders"? Surely these kinds of comments are really quite insensitive and suggest that the government is not really serious. It suggests to a number of Canadians that perhaps this is nothing but symbolic window dressing. Perhaps there are things that are changing. We really do need some explanations from the government. We need to make sure that this is a sincere gesture.

And I would not wish to overlook the Francophones in this country. My good friend Mr. Forest, who died a few months ago, called me about this. He was all for setting up the Institute, but he wanted to make sure this would not in any way diminish the French language. We will therefore have to make Francophones in Canada understand that establishing this Institute will merely add to what is already being done for their language and culture. If we do not give them these assurances, there may be some very negative feelings.

With respect to our aboriginal peoples, they have indicated that they do not want to be considered under this particular bill. We can best show that if we support them, we must support the private members' bill proposed by my colleague from Western Arctic who suggests that a parallel institute be created for aboriginal languages.

Mr. Speaker, after these comments, I would like to say that, together with my colleagues, I am prepared to support this bill, with the reservations I just mentioned.
