On the whole, I believe it is a very important initiative. On the other hand, certain precautions must be taken, and I hope that for once the government will listen.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the Chair. I believe that members on this side of the House, at least in the Liberal Party, have agreed that we would like to start sharing our time in two 10-minute periods, followed by the usual five-minute questions and comments. That is because we have a large number of members who are interested in this bill and who would like to expedite the legislation as fast as possible.

Mr. Speaker,
I know that my venerable House leader did that in order to prevent you from having to listen to another of my tirades for more than a minimum amount of time. That really is not so because he is interested in making the affairs of the House go much smoother. I thank him anyway for standing up and at least giving me an introduction in such a tentative fashion.
We have debated this bill in the past and we have highlighted the pitfalls associated with it. My colleague from the NDP, who is normally very thorough in her analysis of all of the things that go wrong with the bill, or with any bill, has been quite correct to outline many of the drawbacks to this one.
I am at a little bit of a disadvantage, having followed a colleague from my caucus who is very erudite and who is also very knowledgeable in this area. He has given us some very good reasons for supporting the heritage language foundation and heritage languages in general.
One of the things that bothers me as a member of the House, after having gone through committee and debated this bill at second reading, is that what we have seen, both through government action and through some of the debates that have taken place in the House, a picture of a country that is so great and diverse as Canada-I use great in a qualitative fashion, rather than in a geographic sense, because this is a country that has become the host or hostess of the largest number of different peoples throughout the entire world.
My colleague from Winnipeg just pointed out the major language groups. He indicated for the purposes of this House those numbers of Canadians who identified

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
themselves as functioning in a mother tongue other than English or French.
That does not mean that those people identified themselves as being Chinese, Korean, Italian, Portuguese or Spanish. They identified themselves as Canadians whose mother tongue, whose language of function, happens to be the ones that he enumerated.
I draw to the attention of all members the statistics that my colleague presented for consideration. When we are talking about people who identify themselves as functioning in a language other than the ones that are official in this country, the number-again I remind all listeners that it was only a sample-was well past three million Canadians who function in a language other than the two official languages.
It calls to mind what I started to say a moment ago, that a country that is capable of hosting people who still function in other languages, other than the official ones, finds itself with a government which through legislation has demonstrated a most parochial and narrow view of the way its own citizens relate one to the other and the way its own citizens developed the economy of this country and the way in which they establish an opportunity, a bridgehead if you will, with other areas of the world.
My colleague from Winnipeg has pointed out to all of us here who were not aware that we have tens of billions of dollars of trade with countries as a result of the contacts established by those people who function in a mother tongue other than English or French.
Those people would not include individuals like myself whom StatsCanada would not identify as operating in a mother tongue other than English or French, but who comes from one of those other racial or linguistic groups.
If we are serious about some of the statements that the government is making, what we should be doing is examining these kinds of initiatives in the context of the broader government initiative.
The parliamentary secretary for citizenship and multi-culturalism was very proud to point out that this is another step in the establishment of broad multicultural principles which are supposed to govern this country. We have had opportunity to criticize employment equity as a function of those initiatives. We have had opportunity to
criticize and analyse the function of heritage language cuts in that context.
I know hon. colleagues will already have been impressed with the intrinsic value of language. They will also be impressed with the analysis of what happens to policy and what happens to the dictates of commitment to the development of a country and to government policy when, on the one hand, it withdraws funds that allow for the further generation and development of language groups and, on the other hand, it establishes a foundation which has a series of nine purposes that are supposed to do something positive.
Perhaps we are stealing from Peter in order to pay Paul. I am going to be kind, because I saw throughout the parliamentary committees and the standing committee at debate on second reading an opportunity that no one has identified just as yet, that is an opportunity to establish the infrastructure for a truly multicultural policy which should permeate all departments.
We have had the Minister of State for Multicultural-ism and Citizenship and his parliamentary secretary, with great pride outline the fact that now we finally have a separate department for multiculturalism. Presumably that department will flourish, develop, grow, and eventually reflect the demographic reality and diversity that is Canada.
As well we heard her say: "Look, we now have this foundation, the Fleritage Language Institute." The legislative committee on a race relations foundation will present its report next week. We have at least three pillars for the establishment of an infrastructure. The parliamentary secretary and her minister have given us an indication that there may be a parallel or sister foundation for native heritage language programs. There will be four pillars of the development or identification of a much more varied society in Canada.
If we are taking all of these initiatives, why would we start cutting funds that are absolutely crucial to the maintenance of language programs which will allow young boys and girls the opportunity to study a language, thought development, culture, philosophy of life, historical and cultural traditions that emanate from their parents and their family life and to give them an opportunity to discover themselves and do it with pride
October 19, 1990

before or while they integrate into the mainstream of Canadian life?
Why would we withdraw funds that would make it opportune for Canada to generate new Canadians as solid, self-confident, aggressive individuals who see themselves for what they are and who see themselves as part of the whole Canadian mosaic?
I do not know whether hon. members would agree if on one hand they acknowledge that they welcome and in fact encourage such a development and on the other hand they remove the means whereby that development can come to realization.
If I were to spend more time describing why it is that language development is important, I do not know whether the minister opposite who is already very fluent in two languages would not recognize the importance of being fluent in more than two. When I said that we were becoming rather parochial, perhaps I should have been thinking of the minister opposite in terms of what we should be doing when most other countries in the world are encouraging all of their citizens to go to not only the second but a third and fourth language in a global society, in a global economy.
They are taking away funds, $4 million, from something that should be a solid and integral part of where we should be going. While they are removing $4 million from something that could be socially and economically beneficial, they are throwing away, as I said in a statement earlier today, $602 million to poor multinational oil companies for exploration purposes out west.
I think most Canadians and members on this side of the House see an inconsistency that they would like to see corrected, even though they recognize the worthwhile nature inherent in the establishment of such a foundation.
I would hope all members would see this bill for what it is, a first minor step in the direction that we all hope would emanate from the rhetoric coming from the department, a rhetoric that we hope becomes material rather than just empty phrases.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister introduced this legislation I was very encouraged for several reasons, not the least of which
Government Orders
was that I am a unilingual Canadian with all kinds of hopes and aspirations that I would perhaps become bilingual and fears that reality dictates that I may not.
There is always hope.

There is always hope, that is true. I stand here with envy of at least the two people who have spoken before me, knowing that in one instance the speaker is more than bilingual. The fact of the matter is that the way in which the minister first introduced the bill gave me hope that the Canadian tradition of being multicultural, in addition to the other things that have gone on in Parliament and in this country in the creation of the multicultural department, is very encouraging.
My problem is that when it comes down to the reality of it, like so many other things we have seen happen in this country over the last couple of years and what I have seen in the last couple of years in the House, what we really have in the final analysis are some very hollow words. The problem is that the words, hopes and aspirations being generated by a lot of activity on the government side are not and will not come to fruition in anywhere near the grand possibility that is presented within them.
I have received more mail, not only from my own constituency or my own city of Saskatoon but from elsewhere across the country, on the issue of a heritage language foundation and on the issue of heritage languages than I have on any other issue other than the GST. I suppose there is not much use debating the GST at the moment. I certainly want to debate and draw to the attention of other members of the House and yourself, Mr. Speaker, some of the comments that have come to me from people who are concerned about what is happening with the heritage languages foundation.
Their concern is primarily that it seems there has been a tradeoff. That may or may not be the case, but certainly it seems there has been a tradeoff in taking money away from what has been described to me as one of the most valuable educational institutions within Saskatoon and within Saskatchewan, an institute that has over 20 years of experience. The government is taking money away from it and putting it into an institute which will receive funding over a five-year period. It is rather questionable about what will occur after that.

The problem is that these things are not necessarily mutually exclusive and, while it is true that we as New Democrats support the implementation of the institute, it is also true that we decry in the strongest terms the cutbacks in funding to the heritages languages which we have found within our community and which is expressed in far better language by the people themselves who are involved than I possibly could. I have a letter here from the President of the Saskatchewan Organization for Heritage Languages, Shakeel Akhtar, who wrote:
lam writing to you to convey our anger and dismay over the recent federal budget, which completely eliminated funding for all supplementary heritage language schools in Canada.
In Saskatchewan, heritage languages are taught primarily in the out-of-school situation, relying heavily on the goodwill and determination of volunteer language teachers from the particular ethnocultural communities.
These communities make up the mosaic of our city and province.
I also have a letter from a very dear friend of multiculturalism, immigration and the multicultural mosaic of our country, Mr. Mike Kindrachuk, President of the Saskatoon Multicultural Council. He wrote:
On behalf of the 12,000 members of the Saskatoon Multicultural Council and our Multicultural School, I must inform you of our shock and outrage at your decision to completely eliminate operating funding for supplementary heritage language schools.
Such radical decisions should not be made without appropriate consultation -
This is another very important issue involved in this whole discussion: without consultation. This is something which has been repeated over and over to me in so much of the correspondence I have received.
Another important point which was made was that it is questionable whether or not there was a cut in funding to the department. I have seen figures which show it actually got a 15 per cent increase, but there has been some indication that it was cut by 5 per cent. I am not in any position at the moment to determine which of those two figures are important, but I am in a position to point out a letter from Linda Flory who wrote:
We have been informed that the total budget of the Secretary of State has been cut by only 5 per cent. Within this budget the minister cut off the heritage language schools by 100 per cent-
Whether it is a 5 per cent decrease or a 15 per cent decrease, it is a 100 per cent cut to the heritage language schooling which goes on within our heritage communities.
I have another letter from Mr. Thomas Heine of the German community in Saskatoon. Among other things, he wrote:
It was with great disappointment and dismay that I heard about your recent decision to completely cut funding for all heritage language schools -
With regard to the German community, he wrote:
We also note that you are planning to establish a centralized Heritage Language Institute-at a cost of $6.7 million. What would be the purpose of such an institute? We note that very few of the heritage language groups are in favour of such an institute: we prefer to teach languages rather than just study them.
I think that is a very important matter when it comes to this whole discussion. He continued:
Curricula have already been established through the efforts of the various modern language schools across Canada. In the case of the German language schools, graduates are able to obtain international recognition for successful completion of the programs that we have already established.
In personal discussions with Mr. Heine he pointed out that the lingua franca of the German language, the Goethe Institute accepts the levels reached within that heritage language school in Saskatoon. It is very painful to those people as well as others that such drastic cuts have been made.
I have a letter from Mr. Charles Pei of the Edmonton Centre of Chinese Heritage and Second Language Studies.
He says:
I had just returned from the Saskatchewan second heritage language teachers' spring conference in March -held in Saskatoon. I was so surprised by the level of emotion expressed by all participants on the sudden elimination of the Federal government's per student grant to our heritage language schools.
You may not have direct experience with any of these heritage language schools operated after normal school hours by the parents. It is the real community foundation of our multicultural Canada and that is what hurts the feeling of these people so much and they expressed their frustration in the most simple and sincere way a citizen can show. Mr. Speaker, the Jewish community in Saskatoon also wrote me concerning the cuts. The Hindi School of Saskatoon wrote and told me that they were terribly concerned about those cuts. I also received a letter from the Jewish Community Centre in Saskatoon. And, I have here a particularly poignant letter from the Cambodian Association. Listen to this, I will quote from the letter:
We began the the Khmer Language School in the fall of 1989, recognizing the value of retaining the Khmer language and passing it on to our children. But now, after only one year of operation, the School is faced with the threat of having to close because of the Secretaiy of State's funding cuts. It is impossible to collect fees from the students as they and their parents are-
-all very poor and restricted financial ability.
Mr. Rozdilsky wrote to me, on behalf of the Ukrainian Canadian Committee, to express concern over the cuts for heritage language training.
Mr. Speaker, it is not a matter of not building the institute in Edmonton, it is a matter of building the institute in Edmonton, with the academic and research capability that it will obviously have, and it is also a matter of retaining the funding for those heritage languages.
The heritage languages, as has been pointed out by many other speakers, are so important to the future of this country because, if we have the ability to be able to communicate in this new trading situation which is developing in the world in the languages of other countries, which we must retain within our own country through our own citizens, in comparison to the amount of money we have given to the oil companies, the small amount of money invested for this training would be returned many times.
I would like to remind hon. members that there are going to be rallies and demonstrations across the country and there is certainly going to be one here on Parliament Hill on October 27. I would like to remind those, in Saskatoon, who are listening there will also be one in Saskatoon on October 27 on the corner of Third Avenue and 22nd Street.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak on this bill because it gives me an opportunity to talk about a part of our Canadian-ism that is vitally important to me and perhaps even more treasured by me as the daughter of an immigrant to Canada.
Government Orders
We are, indeed, a fortunate nation. We have been wise enough throughout our history to ask of people who come to this country from another culture and with another language that they retain their language and culture and use them to add to the richness, diversity and vibrancy of our Canadian culture. One of the most important ways we have done this is by encouraging the teaching of heritage languages and, in conjunction with the teaching of heritage languages, the teaching of the cultures and an appreciation of the cultures of the countries from which many of our immigrants have come.
For many cultural groups this has meant, through many generations, retaining a sense of attachment to their roots, their background, to the place from which their families originally came and bringing that as a vital and valuable contribution to their Canadianism and, indeed, to the Canadianism of each and every one of us.
I cannot over-emphasize my emotion when I and other members from the Ottawa-Carleton region met with representatives of the 70 heritage language schools in the national capital area. There are 70 schools just on this side of the river. I was touched by their awareness of how important these schools are, not to them and not to their children, but to the total Canadian society. They talked to me about the importance of their children going into the schools and playgrounds of Canada with an understanding of their culture of origin. They told me that sharing that culture with their fellow students or with their playmates wherever they were meant that not only they but the children from the two founding cultures were also finding their lives enriched and made more interesting by the fact that those of immigrant backgrounds were retaining those cultural links.
It has impressed me as well that Canada has a very important international role to play on a number of fronts. One of those that is certainly most important to me is the environment. I do believe we have a leading role to play in developing technology and leading world opinion so that the countries of the world are co-operating together to avoid the destruction of our planet and to ensure the preservation of life on this earth on a more equitable basis than has happened in the past. What more valuable resource to have as we play that role than to have close to one-third of our population now with

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
links and family, cultural and linguistic ties to literally every comer of the earth.
The members from the Ottawa-Carleton schools talked to us about how important the schools are in the integration, not the assimilation, of immigrants into Canadian society. In particular the women are often not out in the workforce and therefore have much greater difficulty learning the language. For many of them their involvement with the school is their best way of becoming integrated into Canadian society, coming in contact with other families and learning one or the other of the Canadian official languages, English or French, and through their children and their children's involvement in the school becoming part of Canadian society more fully than they might otherwise do.
That to me is the importance of heritage languages in our society, not an institute. An institute only serves us well if it is there in support of that grassroots process that involves 150,000 children in this country and many thousands more who are teachers and parents involved in the program. If the institute can provide resources, can assist in the development and preservation of heritage language schools right across the country, I wish it the best, but it is thwarted and doomed to failure if the very grassroots for which it exists are cut off as they have been by this government in cancelling funding for heritage languages.
I want to address one other issue because I think it is of vital importance and that is the failure of the government to recognize that aboriginal languages are not, repeat not, part of the whole package of heritage languages. Aboriginal languages are one of our founding languages and part of one of our founding cultures. Lumping them in in the way they have done in this institute has added another dramatic failure to our lack of recognition of the importance of the aboriginal culture and the aboriginal peoples in Canadian society. We have been through a long and bitter summer. The fact that this bill is passing today without the amendment that would have removed aboriginal languages from heritage languages I think is a shame. We have got to remember that we are the birthplace, we are the place where aboriginal languages exist and whether they continue to exist in this world or not depends on whether we encourage and support their existence in Canada.
If we had one small little plant, or one small little insect, that existed nowhere else but in Canada, we would fight to preserve that with every breath we have. Yet we are failing miserably to protect a living culture that thrives and survives through its languages.
We are failing not only our aboriginal peoples, we are failing our own Canadian society and we are failing world culture by not making a commitment to aboriginal languages we should be making.
I hope the institute is successful but I hope it does not become a tree planted in the middle of an urban environment without enough earth around it for its roots to grow. I hope we do not continue to cut off the roots that make this institute relevant to Canadian society. If we do, we will just have another empty shell that serves no useful purpose, that is there as a nice little token that we can trot out to visitors from abroad.
I want to conclude by saying that the schools in this region have decided this is a serious issue. They want to challenge the government to reinstate what it cut from them this year. They will be holding a rally on October 27 on Parliament Hill and I invite any member in the House to encourage their heritage language schools to join them in spirit, if not in person.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to rise in the House today to speak in support of Bill C-37, an act to establish a Canadian heritage languages institute.
The formation of this institute is an important step toward making Canada a truly multicultural nation. Within this year, some 175,000 immigrants will have become permanent residents of Canada. They will have come from every corner of the globe, bringing with them all the richness and colour of their respective cultures, making Canada a better and more exciting place in which to live.
They form communities within which they celebrate their own religions, festivals, foods, and languages. Some of them open shops, restaurants, and other businesses, giving Canadians a taste of their homeland and a chance to begin to understand what would have otherwise remained foreign.
However, religious affiliation, residence in an ethnic neighbourhood, or even marriage within an ethnic group, do not necessarily keep a minority group culture intact. Language is the single most important element in
October 19, 1990

a culture. Language is the single most effective medium through which to preserve a culture.

Mr. Speaker, studies have shown that if an ethnic group fails to preserve its language, integration quickly and inevitably means assimilation. This is a country that is proud of its multiculturalism and its racial and religious tolerance. However, tolerance is not enough. We must play an active role in creating ways in which our ethnic minorities can preserve their language or their heritage. This would be the role of the Heritage Languages Canadian Institute: to promote heritage languages.
There are, however, a number of questions that remain to be answered. Will this Institute meet the real and concrete needs of our ethnic communities?

The institute would have a mandate to promote the learning of heritage languages, to provide information to the public about heritage language resources, to develop programs to improve the quality of heritage instruction, to assist in the production and dissemination of related materials, to assist in the development of learning standards, to conduct research into heritage languages, to establish scholarly and professional links to further their mandate, and to encourage consultation in matters relating to heritage languages.
Research, consultation, and the establishment of scholarly and professional links are obviously very important aspects of an institute of this kind, but who will ultimately benefit?
There is concern that the institute could lose sight of its responsibility toward the actual ethnic minorities while concentrating too heavily on its dealings with academia. It is possible that, without close scrutiny, the institute could find itself providing assistance, not to the students of heritage languages, but rather to language scholars.
There is danger of the institute promoting programs and disseminating information that never materialize in our ethnic communities. I believe the the government must expect to keep a vigilant eye on the proposed
Government Orders
institute once it becomes reality in order to ensure that its mandate is indeed carried out towards the survival and, hopefully, the enhancement of our ethnic communities.
The second question which we must address is the lack of adequate programs to educate our new Canadians in English or French as a second language. The need for heritage language training is real and, as I have stated, the preservation of ethnic cultures through language serves only to enrich Canada and its inhabitants. However, the need for our new Canadians to understand and to be able to function productively in at least one of our two official languages is a basic one.
It is imperative that those who are granted Canadian citizenship and who do not come from a country where either French or English is widely spoken be provided with the means to successfully integrate themselves into the realities of their new home. It would be appropriate, given the proposals contained in Bill C-37, that the government take steps to ensure the availability of proper second language training for ethnic minorities in tandem with its efforts to ensure the survival of heritage languages.
Another concern with respect to the proposed Canadian Heritage Languages Institute is the issue of the preservation of aboriginal languages. Deleted from Bill C-37's original text when the bill was in committee was a section which included "any aboriginal language" as a heritage language. This was done at the request of the Assembly of First Nations. Obviously, as pointed out by native leaders, aboriginal languages are founding languages of this nation and not heritage languages.
Heritage languages are those that may be retrieved from one's original homeland, but we can never retrieve an aboriginal language. Once an aboriginal language is lost here in Canada, it is lost forever. To help prevent such losses in the future, it would be necessary for the government to establish a foundation or an institute similar to the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute for the purposes of retaining and encouraging aboriginal languages.
My colleague, the member for Western Arctic, has developed a private member's bill, Bill C-269, dealing with this very issue. As with the issue of English or French as a second language for new Canadians, I believe that if the government has the intention of being

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
taken seriously with respect to language issues as a whole, it should consider Bill C-269 very carefully.
In closing, I would like to restate my support of Bill C-37. An institute of the kind proposed by this bill is badly needed in Canada. Every year, Canada attracts more immigrants from countries where the language and culture differ radically from our own. The Government of Canada must continue in its efforts to assist Canadians in the preservation of their cultural and linguistic heritage.
We are all very proud to be citizens of this great country, each one with a desire to be a productive part of society and to help make Canada a better place for all. Equally so, the many diverse customs, religions and languages that have come to Canada are worthy of support, for in our diversity we can find the strength to go forward to break new ground in a land blessed with the freedoms and opportunities which we are so fortunate to enjoy.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments. Debate. The hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak to this important piece of legislation which we call the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute Act. I would like to make a couple of general comments.
I view this legislation, as I hope we all do, as a mechanism or a way and means of consolidating our country's approach to the development of the teaching and learning of heritage languages.
The profile of the use of heritage languages in this country other than English, French and aboriginal languages, to which I will make reference later, is usually an urban profile, but it is not exclusively so. I am sure that in Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, Beauce, Quebec, and Pictou, Nova Scotia, there are heritage languages represented there. We really do have a challenge to address this very valuable asset that we, as Canadians, have. I am very confident, subject again to a comment that I will make in a moment or two, that any investment we put into this as a country will be rewarded many times over.
In my own riding of Scarborough-Rouge River, a rough count shows me that there are approximately 20 first languages other than English and French spoken in the riding. I have heard most of them. That does not
include Jamaican, which many of my constituents will regard as another language and I say that respectfully.
In my own riding executive, just the table officers represent six first languages other than English. That manifests, at least in the part of the country that I come from, the existence of a reservoir, a bank of linguistic ability that can serve our country, not just domestically, but around the world. I am very confident that we will put that to use.
Language, as well, is perhaps the principal vehicle of delivery of culture, something that we regard as very important in Canada. Language is a vital component of that and, to the extent that we wish to foster further the many cultures found in Canada in all their manifestations, we have an obligation to ensure that language, the vital component of that, is buttressed.
This is a note of caution because I do not think we should confuse heritage language with two other elements. Very briefly, I will speak from a point of reference in my own riding of two challenges which developed beyond the realm of heritage language, but which are not unrelated to it.
The first area is the challenge to develop English as second language education, not just for youth, but for adults. There are great challenges in many of our urban centres. Funding appears to be insufficient. We have large numbers of new Canadians. They desperately require first language training. I use English as a second language because in my riding that would be the dominant first language, but French as a second language has equal validity in the province of Quebec and other parts of Canada where French is the principle language spoken on the street.
The second area is the challenge to all of us of integrating new Canadians whose first language is other than English or French. I think primarily of immigrant women. These individuals need access to English and French training so that they may access the many opportunities that the country has for them and for all of us.
I have to take note then of a modest problem we have here in the definition of heritage language. It has been referred to by many other speakers, including the member for Stormont-Dundas who preceded me. That is the inclusion of aboriginal languages.

I rhetorically ask the question of how much consultation really did take place prior to proceeding with this legislation with a view to providing our aboriginal peoples with a sense of security that their languages would receive the attention they deserve and badly need to ensure their survival. It may be construed as an insult that they perhaps were not consulted to the degree that they might have wished. One thing is certain, I would not want our success in pursuing the goals of this particular legislation in any way to detract from other initiatives that must be there to foster the strength and education in the aboriginal terms.
Another challenge that I see from the structure of the bill that must be addressed-at least I believe we are going to have to address it-is that we have many heritage languages, in excess of 25 or 30.1 think there is a challenge to the first directors of this heritage languages institute to ensure that all these languages are addressed equitably and fairly, with some proportionality and a political sensitivity to the presence of all of them.
We do not want to have a Tower of Babel constructed here in the first board of directors. I note that there are only 21 directors. There are a heck of a lot more than 21 heritage languages. I do not envy those who must make the decision as to which languages will be represented on that first board. However, that challenge remains.
The last item I want to take note of is that I hope the government does not hope to choke off this institution by under-funding it. It may look good on paper, but I note that the first year's funding is $800,000 in capital and $500,000 in current expenses. I look at 21 directors and I know how much it costs to move people from one part of Canada to Edmonton. I just have this fear that it will eat up half of that first year's funding just to have its first board meeting.
There are no other mechanisms inserted in the statute to provide funding for all the many good things that this institution will want to accomplish. I caution the government on that. I just have a feeling that the operation is under-funded and there will be many complaints in the months to come about the under-funding. I do not want to by too cynical. I hope the government realizes that it cannot offer what it is now offering and under-fund it. It will have failed in its objective if that is the course it wishes to take.
Government Orders
Having said that, I am happy to include my vote with those supporting this important piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy and honoured to rise and speak on this issue of heritage language.
Before I do so I would like to say a word of thanks and appreciation to the Minister of State for Multicultural-ism on this wonderful and excellent initiative. Certainly the bill to a large extent addresses the issue of heritage languages fairly well in the sense that he is setting up an institute that will be used and will act as a clearing house and agency that will pass on information and deal with the issue of heritage languages from close by or from far away. It is there. I could not help but mention one statement made by a colleague, Shaun Murray. He told me the other day that if he one day became the Prime Minister, one of the things he would do would be to allow every Canadian a one-time deal tax deduction, one trip to a Third World country and back to Canada and look at what we have here in order to appreciate the type of country we have and the type of society in which we live. We can appreciate and see how fortunate we are to live in a caring, compassionate country such as Canada. I am very proud of my Canadian citizenship. I value it tremendously.
There is an area that concerns me tremendously as well as it concerns a lot of Canadians, and that is the issue of citizenship. When it comes to good citizenship, we have to make sure that the opportunities are available and provided to citizens from all walks of life, regardless of their background and regardless of the country from which they come, the colour of face, origin and also that they are provided with the tools to become good Canadian citizens.
When it comes to heritage languages, it is very important to let people learn the language of their own country. Also, I believe it is as important for all new Canadians who come to Canada, including myself, to be able to speak the language of the country that has adopted them, whether it is English, French, or perhaps both languages. That opportunity, as it is right now, unfortunately is not available to all Canadians. In particular, it is not available to newly arrived landed immigrants from different parts of the world, whether from eastern Europe, western Europe or Third World coun-

October 19, 1990
Government Orders
tries, or countries where their people speak languages other than French and English.
English or French as a second language is quite a situation across the country right now. School boards are struggling in order to deal with the high demand for teachers, resources and funds in order to support the school boards to deal with English or French as a second language. They just do not have the resources to deal with that problem.
Here is an opportunity that the Secretary of State has missed. That is to take a leadership role in education. When it comes to English as a second language, it really fits right into what the Minister of Citizenship and Multiculturalism is trying to do, and that is to build a stronger Canada or help to build a stronger Canada. There is a deficiency.
We have done a cross-country check-up. We have called every major school board in every major centre across Canada. Every single school board we contacted told us that they have waiting lists of hundreds and hundreds of people from different parts of the world who want to enrol in a program to learn French or English. They cannot get to these programs. The result is that there will be many people unemployed. As a result of that, they may go on the welfare rolls because they cannot speak the language that will help them to integrate into society. It is a major problem.
On Tuesday next week, we will meet with representatives of school boards from across the country. These representatives will call on the federal government to take some sort of leadership role on the issue and step in to assist the provinces to deal with the issue head on, because the issue needs to be addressed quickly.
We support the bill as opposition members because we believe it is a good bill. It fits in nicely with what we are looking for. We are very disappointed because of the $4 million cut to the heritage language schools, which can affect them quite extensively.
In the Ottawa-Carleton region we have approximately 70 schools that teach heritage languages and the cut would involve 40 per cent of their funding. On average, each school receives approximately $10,000. Four thousand dollars from every school is quite a bit of money when dealing with schools that are operated on a non-profit basis. We are disappointed with that.
The number of children across Canada who benefit from heritage schools is approximately 150,000 to 170,000 students. There are approximately 6,000 teachers involved in providing those kinds of services. That is quite a large number of people who are receiving the benefit of such a program.
The minister ought to be proud of the kind of initiative he has taken on this issue and I would like to thank him.

Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to hear my colleagues, the member for Ottawa Centre and the member for Ottawa West, speak on this because the three of us were involved, along with a lot of other members of Parliament, in meeting with different people from the various heritage language schools in the Ottawa-Carleton area.
These people met with us and their voice was as one. They did not understand why the cuts were made to their heritage language schools. They did not understand or realize the problems they were going to be faced with in trying to raise the money to continue on with these programs.
Most of these programs are taught on a Saturday and they are taught mainly through the large efforts of volunteers within their own particular cultural community. With the many cuts last June in the budget, Mr. Speaker, fund raising, not just for heritage language schools, but for many organizations and non-profit organizations about the country, is putting stress on the availability of the dollar.
The heritage language school is terribly important for these groups within our country. Before I ask my question, I would point out there are three particular areas that really affects them. It detracts from the ability of ethnic minorities to feel a vibrant part of the mosaic because their full participation as individuals belonging to an ethnic group is denied. Heritage language training provides a competitive edge in the international marketplace and heritage language training promotes the understanding of the importance of culture retention. An understanding of the French fact in Canada would be promoted along with immigrant groups.
My question to my colleague for Ottawa Centre is that some months have passed since that meeting. I believe it was something like 16 organizations, if I remember
October 19, 1990

correctly. I have had contact with some of the organizations within my municipality and my riding of Nepean and I would like to know if the member has had any contact with the heritage language groups in his riding, how they are coping with it, and do they see their problems as being eliminated at this point in time?

Mr. Speaker, I can see the clock is getting closer to two o'clock and I want to make sure that in one and a half minutes, at the very most, that I address the concerns of my colleague.
Yes, we have been working with the organizations here. My colleague for Ottawa West, as well as my colleagues for Ottawa South and Nepean, as well from Ottawa Carleton and Ottawa-Vanier, have all been in touch with the school boards and with the heritage schools, and it is a major concern.
It is my hope, on a very positive note, that the minister of multiculturalism will take note of this as he goes through Hansard. They have an excellent opportunity here to make some good announcements and reinstate the $4.1 million cut from the budget in order to allow those schools to deliver the goods and services they are providing to children in the national capital region as well as children across our country.
Once again I thank the hon. member for the good question.

that Bill C-316, an act to amend the Copyright Act (fair use), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to debate my Private Members' Bill C-316 to amend the Copyright Act. I would like to thank those people who have collaborated with me on it; in particular, Pierre Yves Boucher, the executive director and legal counsel of the Association of Colleges and Universities, and Lorraine Flaherty of the Canadian School Trustees Association.
I would also like to express my gratitude to the staff of the Library of Parliament, Monique Hebert and Diane MacMurray for their invaluable advice and assistance in the drafting of this bill.
To date, the bill is supported by the Association of Colleges and Universities of Canada, the Canadian School Trustees Association, The Association for Media Literacy, the Canadian Music Publishers Association, CREPUC, representing university libraries in Quebec, many members of Parliament, numerous school and library boards and various private sector businesses which see this as a reasonable solution to the problems created by the existing legislation.
I would like to note that many of these problems were there before the amendments that occurred to the act were undertaken by this government. However, the increasing militancy of creators and the attention that has been focused on this issue have created a realization, particularly in the education and library fields, that much of what we in our society do with works created by others is illegal.
Teachers across Canada are very much aware of this and their potential liability. In my part of the country, metropolitan Toronto, a teacher in Scarborough had to pay an out of court settlement of $2,000 after a CBC

October 19, 1990
Private Members' Business
employee took the teacher to court for playing a tape of material taken off the television in the classroom.
I am informed that recently a school in Etobicoke had tapes seized and a heavy fine was required to be paid.
School boards and libraries have considered this issue and have sent out directives to their staff. Some boards have even removed the record buttons on VCRs. This means that teachers must limit themselves legally and, if they are very careful, to strict textbook teaching and use of materials that their board has purchased. Otherwise, they could be liable for action such as the two I have referred to.
This is almost impossible for people teaching today. It makes for a very boring and irrelevant classroom. One of the things teachers are taught to do is to try to relate the principles learned in the classroom to the materials in the real world that students are familiar with.
The legislation passed by this House in Phase 1 of the copyright revision modified the law to give creators secure and unequivocal control over their works and thus ensure them compensation. I think that was an important and a very necessary step that has assisted creators, in particular some of our more recent creators in the computer and programming industry and the music industry in ensuring the protection of their property-
Educators, librarians and others-I would say the vast majority of Canadians-recognize the rights of creators. Indeed, they are strong supporters of Canadian creators. No one that I have met wants to deny creators compensation or the right to earn a living from their work, or indeed control over the public presentation of their works. Many educators are also creators. However, there is a serious lack of balance in this legislation and some very serious access problems which the bill we have before us today attempts to address.
The minister and the previous minister of communications promised to bring in certain exemptions for education and libraries, and consultation has taken place with certain representatives from those groups. A number of exemptions from the legislation have been drafted.
My bill does not address these exemptions and simply assumes the minister will bring these in, in due course, although we have been advised that these are imminent for several years now. Some of the recommendations that are in these proposed exemptions are as follows. For example, it will permit the manual copying of work. Writing a poem on a blackboard is technically illegal. The exemptions the minister will bring in will also permit teachers and students to copy copyright works in examination questions and answers. Obviously much of this is going on now. It will permit the playing of a radio or television set in the course of teaching and research. It will permit live performances by teachers or students in the course of teaching and research.
I am sure almost everyone here who attended school took part in a classroom play at one point or another. Did you realize that this was illegal?
It will also permit the playing of a record or an audio tape in a classroom and the off air taping of news and public affairs programs.
I think those are essential, and I think we all recognize that certainly they are going on right now in the classrooms of this nation.
The bill before us addresses all those works that are not in the repertoire of a collective or the lists in a society or association as referred to in the act that has the power to license and permit the use of works. It addresses everything that a collective does not have power over.
Seventy-eight per cent of the works used in Canada are not from Canadian sources. There is a vast amount of audio, visual and print material available which is not controlled by collectives and unlikely to be.
For example, many professionals such as lawyers do not mind people copying their work. We as politicians very seldom mind people copying our letters and distributing them, so we will certainly not be joining collectives. Fair use would apply in all those situations, as well as for foreign materials, where creators would not feel that the market was not large enough or were not desirous of obtaining remuneration. If they did, they would join the collective.
October 19, 1990

What this bill will do is clarify the rules for teachers, librarians and other users including ourselves, businesses and people in our society who are users of works created by others.
Works will be available for use through a collective which can license institutional users and grant permission for use on an equitable and fair basis, or it will be subject to the fair use provisions outlined in this bill.
These fair use provisions are taken directly from American legislation. Essentially what they do is allow reproduction and use of material, provided there is no personal profit and it is used for teaching, review, legislative or judicial proceedings, research, criticism, comment or newspaper summary.
It also provides for a defence of fair use in an action for infringement of copyright and requires destruction of broadcast materials that are reproduced within 120 days from the day the copy is made.
As I stated before, 78 per cent of works used in Canada are not Canadian. Most of these materials come from the United States. Implementation of this bill would mean that the same rules as apply in the United States would cover most works, unless the creators have established or joined a collective or licensing body registered in Canada and made their works available and the terms and conditions of use known.
I think this is very reasonable, since Canadian teachers have been successful in obtaining permission to use American material simply by writing and asking American television networks, magazines and so on whether they could have permission to use their materials in accordance with the fair use provisions.
The impact of this bill on education and librarians will be very positive in clarifying the issue. It is also most important that provincial ministries negotiate agreements with the collectives that have been established as soon as possible, so that works that are listed in the repertoire of collectives are available to educators and librarians on a fair basis. This will allow those creators who wish to receive remuneration for their works to receive it and will allow people to use these works.
The Minister of Communications should also bring forward the exemptions to the copyright legislation that have been agreed to by the consultative committees on educational and library uses. These are important com-
Private Members' Business
ponents of a total package on copyright that our educational and library system can live with.
This bill will provide a great deal of assistance to individuals, governments and private companies that must communicate. Under the existing legislation users are infringing copyright, with the exception of fair dealing, unless they have received the permission of the copyright owner of any work except for the purposes of private study, research, criticism, review or newspaper summary. That has been interpreted very narrowly by the courts as being individual private study. It does not permit the making of multiple copies for classroom use, or for sharing with others, or public performance, or display of work.
We in Parliament are constantly violating copyright legislation. Those of us who stand in this House and read from newspapers or magazines are publicly performing works and violating the law technically. Those of us who copy news items in our householders and circulate them without obtaining prior permission are violating the legislation. Of course Quorum is technically illegal, as are other news clipping services unless they have obtained permission. If we copy articles from Hansard for public circulation, even of our own speeches, this is technically illegal.
Some members have never run into this issue and may think that there is no real problem because nobody in their right mind would require permission or would object. On the contrary, The Toronto Star has a policy that refuses permission to politicians to use pictures and news items they own. I ran into this last year. I could not use a picture of myself, my daughter, and the Yamagami family from my riding who had a disabled child and I helped with an immigration issue. The Toronto Star owns that picture.
This of course would still occur, but they would be registered with a collective and we would at least know what the rules are. As far as those newspapers that do not mind are concerned such as The Ottawa Citizen or have their own rules that allow members to use their material, at least we would know what the name of the game was and we would be able to use the material, so there would be clarity.
If you, Mr. Speaker, have a public meeting or publicly display a picture or a diagram or any work created by someone else, you may be violating the law unless you

October 19, 1990
Private Members' Business
have the permission of the creator. Under my bill, if the work is not in the repertoire of a collective where you can find out what the rules are, the concept of fair use will apply unless you want to use it for commercial purposes. For commercial purposes you would have to obtain copyright permission from the owner.
As I have mentioned, educators are in a particularly difficult position. Multiple copying for classroom use is currently illegal, unless there is an agreement with a collective. However, few provinces have these agreements. Quebec is the only province in which the use of collectives has been developed enough for boards of education to be able to go and obtain an agreement with a collective. The rest of the provinces are in a state of negotiation. It is a very difficult situation now to obtain permission.
I worked on a teaching project with a number of other teachers as part of a course. We decided to try to find out if one could get permission. Our project was a project in which we were studying police drama. We wanted to look in particular at this one unit on the program Night Heat, so I tried to get permission to tape Night Heat and use it in the classroom.
I was passed around to eight different people and each one of them said: "Go ahead and do it. We don't care". I said: "I wanted to do it legally. Our board says that we have to obtain copyright permission. This is the same throughout Ontario. We are working on this teaching unit. I need to obtain it legally". I went through the vice-presidents of CTV. I went through everybody. Finally I found the company that represented doctors and lawyers across Canada which owned the rights to Night Heat. I was able to send a letter to it stating when I was going to tape it, when it would be destroyed and so on. The company agreed, and there was no charge. When the day came when I wanted to tape it and I had made the arrangements, it was bumped for a hockey game. After all that effort, I could not use it.
Our bill will set out clearly for teachers and others what fair use is, and put those conditions that they want, namely, no commercial use and destruction after 120
days, in the legislation. It would be far easier for everybody.
The universities encounter many similar problems. In order to get around this law, students are having to line up at copy machines in libraries. I am familiar with a number of graduate students. Teachers will say the periodical article is in the library students will have to make their own copies. Students are spending as much as $20 a week getting these copies. They are lining up. They can only have the periodical article signed out for 20 minutes, so they are at machines in line-ups copying the article. It is completely counterproductive.
Librarians usually pay $8,000, and some even $25,000, to get periodicals. The idea is that they are used by people in the field. The people who submit to them very seldom get any kind of large remuneration. It is an honour to be published in these magazines and the whole idea is that they should be used. Because of the problems with the copyright legislation, university librarians feel they cannot do it. If the periodical is registered with the collective with the terms of use there, it will be clear. If not, it will be fair use.
Similarly, businesses run into this. One thinks of things that are put out by the Royal Bank, for example, such as a newsletter. It does not mind it being copied and circulated. It is a great honour that its material is circulated and respected. This is another example of someone who does not mind. There are many examples.
What is in this bill for creators? It continues to give creators clear and unequivocal rights to their works, subject only to the exemptions that the minister brings forward. It provides a strong incentive for creators to join collectives if they want remuneration for any of those non-commercial uses permissible under the fair use provisions. It will make the collectives stronger and more viable.
In conclusion, I think this bill will provide for the establishment of a reasonable and balanced approach to the issue of copyright legislation in Canada. I greatly appreciate the support of the House in referring it to the communications committee for further consideration.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   COPYRIGHT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to respond to the speech by the hon. member for St. Boniface.
The present copyright legislation in this country consists of an act drafted in 1921, proclaimed in 1924, and subject to interpretation by the courts. Until quite recently, the legislation had never undergone substantial review. When I hear remarks about confusion, lack of vision and delays, I fully agree with the hon. member since the Liberal Party was in power at the time and, as usual, lacked vision, caused all kinds of delays, and created this confusion. This was typical of the Liberal government throughout its mandate, I may add!
During all those years of Liberal government, we saw, I might say, the birth of radio, television, photocopy machines, tape recorders, videocassette recorders, computers, satellites and various devices for information storage and retrieval. All these technologies have contributed to increasing the use of works protected by copyright.
These new technologies have to a very large extent been instrumental in creating works protected by copy-
October 19, 1990

right. They not only helped produce these works but also provided new ways of using them, and as a result, opened new markets, thus increasing opportunities for pecuniary remuneration in exchange for such use.
However, these technologies also made it possible to make repeated use of protected works without obtaining permission from the copyright owner. For instance, we can easily reproduce a TV program at home by using a videocassette recorder, and it is practically impossible for copyright owners to control how the program is used. Consequently, new technologies have created a host of legal problems, some of which require solution through legislation. That is why the 1924 Copyright Act was partially amended in 1988 by Bill C-60 and by the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement Implementation Act.
In 1988, nine specific amendments were made to the Copyright Act. The maximum fine for criminal offences was raised from two hundred dollars to one million dollars; specific protection was extended to computer programs and moral rights were reinforced to protect the reputation of the author of a work; a public exhibition right for artistic work was created; the link between copyright and drafting was clarified; choreographic work was protected, whether or not it had a story line; and finally, the obligation to obtain a licence for the production of sound recordings was abolished and the application of royalties negotiated on the market was allowed.
Furthermore, Bill C-60 encouraged the creation of corporations for the collective administration of copyright or associations of copyright owners, and provided for regulations in this respect. These licensing bodies, based on a concept that has worked satisfactorily in the music industry for over 50 years, will now be able to operate in all copyright sectors and negotiate the granting of licences with users of works protected by copyright. In exchange for payment of reasonable royalties, they will give users quick and easy access to works protected by copyright. If the licensing body and the user cannot agree on what constitutes a fair royalty, either party may apply to the Copyright Board to fix the amount. Amendments to the Copyright Act have also expanded the jurisdiction of the Copyright Board.
As a result of the amendments to the Copyright Act under terms of the Canada-United States Free Trade Implementation Act, cable operators are required to compensate the holders of copyrights for the re-broad-
Private Members' Business
casting of distant radio and television signals, both Canadian and American.
The amendments which I have just mentioned represent the first step in an effort to update a 66 year old legislation. The Government is determined to continue reviewing the copyright legislation and to implement some of the most urgent amendments which have been favourably and even enthusiastically received by both creators and users.
As it progresses, however, this review brings to light new aspects which, over time, become increasingly relevant and significant, and call for our immediate attention. They are sometimes basic issues or matters of an administrative or technical nature.
A number of these amendments are necessary to meet international requirements concerning copyright or to place Canada on the same footing as its main trading partners. The purposes of other amendments are to update the Copyright Act and to rid it of such terms as "mechanical reproduction" and "perforated rolls". Bill C-316 which the Hon. Member for Don Valley-North introduced and which we are dealing with offers a good example of copyright related issues.
I share the concern of the Hon. Member for Don Valley-North and appreciate her efforts to find a solution to the sensitive problem of the use by teaching establishments of works protected by copyright legislation.
Bill C-316 suggests one way of dealing with exceptions when implementing the Copyright Act, particularly when the permission of the copyright's owner and the payment of royalties are no longer required because a given use is deemed to be fair, pursuant to the standards set in the legislation.
Generally speaking, Bill C-316 is aimed at giving various users access to copyrighted works when such access is not possible under a general licence, that is when the licence giving access to a wide array of copyrighted works cannot be secured. This is why the bill advocates setting up group management companies which authors should join. Still a number of problems related to the bill and external factors make it necessary to take a closer look at the bill before passing judgment on it.
Bill C-316 now provides exceptions in the case of certain users, particularly teachers and researchers. It advocates a radical change concerning both form and

October 19, 1990
Private Members' Business
substance with respect to the fair use concept embodied in the Copyright Act. To some extent the bill goes beyond the discussions which creators and users such as librarians and teachers have had in recent years. The bill may not reflect these discussions because they are part and parcel of the review process and must be taken into consideration in any Copyright Act amendment.
Reviewing copyright provisions has always been a complex and controversial undertaking, if only because of the balance which the Copyright Act must restore between creators and users of copyrighted works. These exceptions are particularly delicate because they can seriously upset the balance if they go too far or not far enough. One of the best ways to be mindful of the delicate nature of the amendments is to see to it that both creator and user are involved in the policy drafting process. That is precisely what the government has done.
In 1987 and 1988 the Department of Communications set up two legislative committees to go over the exceptions which might be included in the copyright legislation. One dealt with exceptions concerning libraries, the other covered exceptions related to the teaching profession. When the two committees began their hearings, creators and users were sitting around the same table but they had strongly diverging views. Users wanted wide-ranging exceptions, first to gain free access to works required for teaching and research, second to be in direct contact with library patrons. Sure enough, creators would have none of this because they felt that these exceptions would encroach upon the rights they had been enjoying all along. I believe that after lengthy and sometines very vociferous debates the parties finally reached common grounds of sorts.
The advisory committees agreed that, instead of widening the scope of the fair use principle, the new legislative provisions would include special exemptions for libraries and schools. Therefore schools and libraries would no longer face the complex problem of having to decide whether a given activity would be deemed to be fair use by a court.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak in this debate today on Bill C-316, put forward by the member for Don Valley North, and to be presenting some of the views from my colleague, the member for Okanagan-Shuswap, who could not be with us today. He is attending to affairs in his riding, as you know, Mr. Speaker.
We do have some concerns and comments obviously about this legislation. I appreciated some of the earlier comments that a speaker made regarding how our contemporary world with its new and modern technology has placed great demands on government regulators to try and catch up in many ways with technology and laws relating to many very important issues. For instance, there is the use of VCR's. I know some constituents who have recorded a number of your memorable rulings, Mr. Speaker, and it is something that you would be concerned about in terms of copyright legislation.
There are the simple things which take so much for granted now, such as the photocopier or the fax machine. All of them may make us technically commit illegal activities in our offices. Many people, of course, would not be familiar with these machines.
In any case, Bill C-316 certainly addresses some serious matters that fall between the rights of creators, artists, and what have you, and the rights of users. That is chiefly, and most importantly, the need to balance these rights for the public good.
At this point we are opposing this legislation as it stands and I will make three quick points in review of our position and then make recommendation for your guidance.
The bill is flawed in its intent in the issues it seeks to address and by lack of a precise definition of certain terms. Clarity of thought and purpose is very important here. Of course, we have to say how important that is in all government legislation.
We say further that the problem faced by educators would be best served by a clause covering the sponta-
October 19, 1990

neous use of material, namely, that as part of negotiated agreements, educators would be able to use articles from newspapers and magazines, combining fair use with just remuneration, something my party has been committed to for some time.
My third point is a matter of time. Overhauling copyright legislation is tough business to be sure, requiring complex and detailed legislation, but the government has made a tough situation tougher for all concerned by not proceeding in a timely way with Phase II of the copyright legislation.
The minister has committed himself to bringing in Phase II twice in 1989. In May, 1988, his predecessor promised Phase II within a few months. It has now been five years since an all-party unanimous committee of the House requested a comprehensive overhaul of copyright laws. It is certainly not the only legislation that probably needs some overhauling.
The minister certainly enjoys his portfolio, but the job confers responsibilities. Full and comprehensive copyright reform is one of them. We know the time we had to wait for a museums policy from the minister. It is an indication that whoever is in charge of the minister's schedule should try to put copyright legislation on Monday's page so that we can give some attention to it.
Our recommendation is this: Because the bill concerns matters of importance, the bill needs more debate. The issues it touches on are important and are certainly worthy of further examination. Because we want the government to get on with the full and comprehensive copyright reform that the House and many others have recommended, we are certainly in full support of referring the matter of the legislation to a legislative committee in the interest of expediting full and comprehensive copyright reform in Canada. Let us hope that this legislation is a step in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to rise and say a few words with respect to this Private Member's Bill, Bill C-316. For me, it points out once again the critical importance of the Private Members' Hour because it is the hour where private members, after often long hours and diligent work, are able to being an issue to the attention of the whole Parliament.
Private Members' Business
As you know, Mr. Speaker, for all the years that you have sat here and the somewhat lesser years I have sat here, that was never ever done. Private Members' Bills were talked out by the hundreds. At the end of the hour, they were simply lost. When we became the government in 1984, we pushed hard and changed those Standing Orders. Now, a certain number of bills have to come to a vote.
This bill did not get on that list where they have to come to a vote, but the excellent work done by the member for Don Valley North has got us to the point where, by consensus, we agree in the House that this matter is so important that it should go on to the standing committee for further study and review.
I want to commend the member for Don Valley North because Parliament can be a very frustrating place, even more frustrating for members on the back-bench on the government side. So much of what we do in the caucus and in the committees never gets reflected in public. Whereas opposition members-and we were the same when we were in opposition-can stand up and take positions and promote them forcefully in public. On the government side we have to do it quietly behind the scenes in the committees. It is always frustrating for government back-benchers and I am sure the member for Don Valley North is very proud, and deservedly proud, of the work she has done on this bill.
There are many people that back this bill in its entirety and it reflects a broad view in our society. It is certainly worthy of detailed study. As previous members have spoken, it is a question of balancing the interests of creators with the interests of people who want to us it, especially for educational purposes. There is no doubt that none of us would ever recommend that we go out and take food from farmers without adequate compensation, or a car from a car manufacturing plant. It is the same with creators of works, especially software and other valuable educational works.
This bill will be an occasion for the standing committee to take a look at it in great detail, bring witnesses in, and further concentrate our minds, as legislators, on this topic. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, speaking for the government, I am pleased to be able to ask this House for unanimous consent that I might put the following motion.

October 19, 1990
Private Members' Business
I move:
That Bill C-316 be withdrawn and that the subject matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
